review:
[h1]Excitement gives way to obligation[/h1]

[h2]In short, here are my issues with the game:[/h2]

- It's philosophically incongruous. Environmentalism is a core tenet of the game, but the base gameplay mechanics encourage the player to hoover up any and all non-renewable resources on every island visited.

- I've never found a reason to re-visit an island.

- Exploration is exciting and rewarding at first. Every island feels new and interesting. But after awhile, you'll realize how much repetition there is, and increasingly skip entire islands. In other words, nearly 2000 islands is too many. I'd say there's only 200 islands worth of content right now. (That's still a lot; there are some very cool ones!)

- The player is told directly by onscreen text to "purge the corruption," which involves killing sapient mushroom creatures that are capable of fear, pain, toolmaking, and only fight in self-defense. Until you kill them, all other interactions with these "corrupted" islands (like building or gathering resources) are directly blocked by the game's non-diegetic text.

- Purging corruption and restoring ecosystems soon becomes a chore and obligation, done only for the exclusive rewards and plot progression. Instead, the player should want to do these things because they serve the player's own goals, through the gameplay mechanics themselves. I've never seen the corruption spread to a new island, and even if it did, with so many uninfected islands still available, it wouldn't negatively affect me. So, I have little real motivation to stop it.

- The more you learn, the LESS interesting and fun the game becomes. For example, (spoilers) [spoiler] once you learn that the frescoes, anchors, knowledge stones, and life fruits are about the only things worth collecting, you'll skip any island that doesn't have them. And once you've collected all the frescoes in a biome, the game directly tells you that there's nothing more to collect. So you'll probably skip new Fresco islands from then on, even if they otherwise look interesting. (The 5 minute buff you get as a consolation prize is essentially worthless.) [/spoiler]

-Pyrologic (logic gates) comes very late in the game, and cannot be used to automate anything useful like farming or ranching. Just doors and lights. So I don't see the point of it unless they add useful stuff later.

-Fast travel exists, but because you can't bring your base island with you, I don't see that there's much point to it. I just ended up making multiple home bases.

[h3]Small issues:[/h3]

- Hovering the cursor over a resource icon does not reveal its name, sometimes making it hard to know what recipes require. I shouldn't have to go to the wiki to find out what something is called. But this would be an easy fix.

-So many things require charcoal, but it's an uncommon and non-renewable resource. I was constantly desperate for more in a way that wasn't fun, and had to forgo many sketches. This will likely be fixed.

-The enduring mystery of "where did everyone go?" is good but never has a resolution. However, I played in early access, so this too will be likely be added later.

[hr][/hr]

Aloft has some good ideas and is initially exciting to play. Really though, I see this game being most useful in inspiring the creation of other, better exploration-based games. 

Imagine instead a game where restoring an island's ecosystem would help you not once, but continuously. Imagine beating back the corruption like fighting on the front lines of a war, with every restored island a victory; one that can be taken away if you don't properly defend it. And imagine having NPCs, both military and civilian, that will live or die based on your decisions. Exploration could still be important, leading to new weapons or techniques to help fight the war.

Or, combine this game with some of the best ideas from the Ur Quan Masters. Play it. With 3800 planets and even less variety than Aloft's islands, you might think it's worse. It's not. The point is that the player must find all the proverbial needles in the haystack, by putting together clues from high and low, and carefully negotiating with NPCs to tease out information, make careful notes, and really think about what to do. Sometimes, multiple sources lead to the same result, so you don't have to play perfectly. I printed out the star chart and was drawing on it with a ruler to find things - a lot of fun.

I guess I'm still searching for a game that will scratch the same itch as Zelda: the Wind Waker. Enough people hated the sailing and dredging in that game, that Nintendo greatly reduced it for the HD remake. Not me; I loved it and wanted more. I can't really say why.

Not every game is for everyone. They shouldn't be. I think Aloft is not quite targeting the sort of itch for exploration that I have. I guess my search will continue.

review:
Aloft has a LOT of potential. It has some really interesting mechanics, like traveling between islands and navigating with an island, also really liked the cute art style. However, there are a few things holding it back for me right now.

The mechanics are not explained very well in-game. I personally didn't struggle with this since I'm an experienced survival game player, but I could see newer players having a harder time. Since Aloft is presented as a “cozy survival” game, I can imagine people who don't usually play survival games giving it a shot and struggling to figure things out.

The game is also VERY buggy. My PC can run games like Monster Hunter Wilds on high settings very smoothly, yet Aloft was extremely scuffed for me. Nothing was going above 60% usage in my task manager with other stuff running on the side, so the performance issues really seemed to come from the game rather than my PC.

As of right now, it's difficult for me to recommend Aloft, but it has a lot of potential. I hope the studio takes the feedback from reviews into account and continues polishing the game, because there are some really cool ideas here.

review:
This is a mixed review after 30 hours of play. 

I find that the game itself is and can be very beautiful and peaceful. Building up your island feels very rewarding, however the building itself is one of the worst in any game I've played. 

Progression as well feels poorly done. 
 The systems make me feel like the devs couldn't decide on which system they liked and ended up mashing them together.

Farming and animal husbandry is nice, animals are cute and you can pet them. However animals can disappear and the smaller critters (while adorable) have very limited animations and no movement making them feel largely lifeless. 

There is very little explanation or guidance to how you do things, what your doing, or why. Also there is very little lore and no real storyline.

Exploration is cool and you find some interesting abandoned villages and neat puzzles or obstacle courses, however many islands have little of worth or value and begin to feel repetitive 

As far as crafting goes there are some cool mini games to crafting but there are also some that where best left on paper like early game cooking water which needs to be done manually via a mini game that gets very repetitive and gives about 5 water per minute.

Altogether this is a pretty game that has some nice peaceful moments but ultimately feels disorganized by to many ideas and systems being mashed together. As it's still in early access I hope the devs can streamline the experience into a more pleasurable and reward time.

review:
Steam needs to add a "Meh" recommendation option for games like this. The game is what it tries to be, but that's all it is...a basic run of the mill exploration game with no rime or reason to it other then to "be" those genre tags. The TLDR, if you are looking for something interesting to play, this isn't it. You build to build, you farm to farm, and you explore to achieve those 2 goals. That is it (from what I have seen).

To start with, the game doesn't really explain much of anything. Why are you here? What happened to everything/everyone? Why are you doing what you are doing? Who knows lol. Things just are. You are slapped into the game with no explanation of anything and that doesn't just apply to the world environment either, it applies to game mechanics and resource collecting as well. Some stuff is explained with tooltips or popup icons when you look at a resource, but not everything. It took me 8 hours before I realized you need to use the "dorkips" tool to get "turf" by stabbing the ground in order to make a roof -_- lol. And on the subject of tools, the game has like 10 of them, and you are constantly swapping them in and out because the hotbar only has 8 slots. It's extremely annoying.

The exploration is mainly resource and knowledge stone hunting, very little exists outside of that. Because of that, most islands are generic resource fillers with one or two interesting places to check out with maybe a puzzle or two to solve in each map section. I've explored through the main 4 sections of the first zone and there is nothing to motivate me to continue. The game has no storyline, no fun/exciting/cool things to unlock...and if it does it does a poor job presenting that to you. The puzzles are nice but in some cases it's just too much work for such a small reward. All in all, it feels like a crafting recipe unlock simulator and everything it tries to be is merely just a means to accomplish that.

The game is indeed a cozy sim with exploration and farming/building. But in order to do most of it, you have to spend tens, if not hundreds of hours to unlock recipes and explore in order to make anything worthwhile and by the time you reach the point where you got a decent amount of things unlocked to build and decorate with...you have no reason to even play the game anymore because once you build what you like...there is literally nothing else to do.

The game is neat, but I can't recommend it for anyone who want's something more then a basic building simulator.

EDIT: Realized I never talked about the gameplay. It's still good! It's just bad performance keeps me from enjoying it and takes me out of the experience. Let's hope the performance update (which is the next early access update as far as I know) fixes these issues.

I've been following this game for a long time and just decided to pick it up again on a whim.
Performance has always been an issue with this game:
- models aren't loaded in at game start, and the loading is not asynchronous so the game will freeze for however long it takes to load the new-to-session model, so if it's on a hard drive, that's on the order of several frames, seconds if there's lots of new-to-session models
- if lots of buildables are present in an area, the game chugs a bit

However, since I played last, performance is significantly worse:
- if a corrupted or wasteland island is present in the render distance, regular islands textures(at least, I think it's the textures) will flicker to black for a frame or two and then turn back to normal. My drivers are updated.
- in general the framerate is just a lot worse no matter where I am in game. I don't have hard numbers on this as I didn't see the need to test back then.

If you want to build a pretty base and not do much else, this game will work, but you could probably do that elsewhere. 

PROS: 
+ aesthetics: some of the animations are awkward, but I do like the aesthetic choices in the game. it's very pretty and cohesive. animal friends are cute. building bases can be pretty and intricate, though this is available in other games, that doesn't make it less fun here.
+ some bugs but I didn't find anything gamebreaking.
+ gliding trials were decently fun. 
+ bringing your base around with you is, in concept, convenient. 

CONS: 
- not very deep, same tasks repeat often. 
- you are both physically railroaded and metaphorically railroaded. 
- backtracking is a massive pain in the ass. 
- environment restoration is kind of a chore after the first few times. you just run around doing the same three things, shove some animals somewhere, and then hug a tree. 
- bringing your base around with you is, in practice, a pain in the ass because it's slow as fuck and you can't really backtrack with it. 
- you'll end up a little disheartened because the game could be so much cooler and it's just not. 
- you're not rewarded for exploring in a genre which should be about exploration. 

The game is pretty and I do enjoy the concepts. The gliding feels natural and once you get the hang of combat it's decent, though not deep. I think there's some fun to be had, but the central repeat pretty quickly becomes stale. 

While you can progress forwards between island clusters easily thanks to the headwinds, going back with your slow as fuck dirt clump is a big pain in the ass. If you're like me and refuse to leave behind any possible animal friends, this quickly becomes a chore. 

There's just not... much to do, really, especially for 25USD. You get pretty much all possible resources for your first tier of environments by the second island cluster, and you've still got a ways to go. You just kinda gotta keep... going... and you're wondering why. Sure, you can unlock new techs - but what's the point of them? You don't access new resources or new mechanics. A lot of filler and fluff and not much else to do.

If I compare this to other survival games, too, I realize that while the environment was pretty, I also got bored of the linear progression quickly. I like getting to explore different environments and obtain different resources from them, such as in Subnautica, where different biomes have vastly different resources and you'll have to explore far to get everything you need. I like wandering off in Subnautica and somehow ending up miles from home deep in a chasm dying to a sea monster. Here, you're railroaded between clusters of islands with a single type of environment and therefore a single set of resources and enemies. There's no side tangents, no way to explore outside of what the game railroads you onto. 

Similarly, while I was excited to get to restore the environments of islands, I realized pretty quickly that there's no real direction to them. You slap some trees and plants and critters in and call it good. There's no "oh well this island needs more butterflies because of XYZ" or "that island needs some frogs because it has water" or even "lizards do well on sunny islands so if you pair lizards with some grasses you get a bonus" nope you just kind of toss whatever you want wherever you want. And it's pretty! But I would love a little more puzzle, or a reason for me to collect animals as I go along. I was so excited to have a big stash of animals I could bust out when an island needed specifically ladybugs because of a niche or whatever and... nah, I just put whatever I want. Which. That's fine, I guess. The ecologist in me is dying a little. But it could've been cooler. 

I think my central issue with the game is that there is no reward for exploration in what is inherently an explorative genre. While tech progression has some side branches, it's not super deep - so while there are small rewards for exploring off the beaten path and finding some nice side chest or lost atlas piece that reveals a hidden area, it's not... huge. It's nothing that you wouldn't have gotten from just doing the next main cluster of islands. The game doesn't reward me for delving into it, when that's the whole point of survival/adventure to me. 

I will say - though I am disappointed by the essential issue in this game (lack of depth), the gliding is smooth and enjoyable. The island piloting mechanics make sense and are approachable. The game functions fine, mechanically.

There are no bugs stopping me from playing this game, and it's pretty, but the biggest issue is there's just no reason for me to play it. I don't sit down at my computer excited to boot it up. It's kind of disappointing in how it could be so much more.

review:
I bought a couple copies of this game to play with my young daughter. She really likes it, and I don't hate it. However, we seem to have run into a wall with progression. We keep exploring new islands but never discover anything new. We can't craft anything to progress past the "storm wall", which seems to be the avenue for progression. I don't know if we are missing something, or if this is just the early access content that's available. 

As an example, we need to craft a "cure" to cleanse a tree island, but we can't craft it yet, and the research station requires materials that we have never seen to advance.

At this point, the game is good for a few hours of fun, but at that point it becomes repetitive and frustrating that you can't progress. So, I can't give it a positive recommendation at this point. I will continue to monitor future updates and if the game improves I will come back and modify my review.

In its current state, I can’t recommend the game. However, I would keep an eye on it as it approaches its 1.0 release. When that will be is unclear, but the potential is definitely there.

review:
This is a painfully slow experience with endless railroading and time gating, with nothing interesting to do on most of the islands. There is no freedom to be found in this game, and hardly any variety of content. The best thing you can do is build a nice house and decorate with animals and such, but plenty of games have that with better gameplay features.

This is bad even for early access, and should not have been released in this state.

The gameplay loop consists of the following: (After you make your glider and island)

1: Fly your slow as dirt clump to a cluster of islands.
2: Visit all the islands and hope they have research points and seeds on them. Clear the infected islands (this is required) and renew the central island's ecosystem. [i]You also have to watch the cutscene for the fruit EVERY TIME. And it's not a fast cutscene.[/i]
3: Do this 3 more times to complete the sub area you're in so you can get the ALSO REQUIRED tree point at the end.

After that you go to the next area and repeat the same steps, visiting and repairing every island. It's a slow and tedious process. Also, if you accidentally miss something, or you think you can move on because your islands suck... well enjoy backtracking against an eternal headwind, because you will not have enough insight to progress any farther in the game. It's also strange to put a wind direction system into the game at all when the wind never changes direction.

You also HAVE to unlock everything in the skill tree in order to progress. I don't know what the point of having branching paths to unlock is if you only really get one or two things before having to go to the other branch just to continue.

This is absolutely shameful to charge money for what is basically a demo.

That being said, there is potential here... but it needs A LOT of time in the oven, and a revamp to allow more freedom and variation of content. I'd like to see more variety in what can spawn early as well. It seems they've broken their game up into "rings" that are unique zones with unique spawns. The problem is, finding only corn and wheat for 10 hours is boring. I'd much prefer if biomes were randomized in some way.

There is clutter everywhere, and research falls behind early on making you back track to get stuff once you unlock the items needed. Back tracking in this game is not fun, it takes a long long long time to sail back to previous locations. 

So what used to be a very "zen" type relaxing game turned into complete frustration entering the 2nd biome. I can only imagine the mess the 3rd is in, but I'm not exactly compelled to carry on at this point. I very much liked the earlier version of this game I feel like they went wrong a long the way.

review:
I used to love this game.  Played through to the teapot four times!  I loved being an ecosystem engineer with my mobile clinic of plants, animals and insects to rescue degraded islands.  And most of all, loved the AGENCY I had as a player.  Sure, I had to hit up the special unlock islands but other than that I could visit the rest of the game world in any order.

The Bloom & Blight update nerfed a lot of player agency.  The base side of things (building, crafting, farming) is still good when you finally manage to unlock the techs.  But getting those unlocks is quite regimented, and a bit harsh.  Progression may look like a tree, but it acts more like a numbered checklist.  There are step-by-step guides on the workshop to teach the ideal unlock order but even then you'll be forced to choose between two timely and essential unlocks.  For example: combat buffs from cooking -OR- farming sheep.  Make a wrong choice and progression is on hold until you pass the time-consuming 'visit these specific islands in this order before proceeding' chore.  

In my house we've started calling Aloft "Backtrackia."  That's the effect of the restrictive progression system.  A lot of time spent sailing backwards to the islands with stuff we weren't allowed to make use of when we first passed through the area.

If you are tolerant of all the gate keeping it's otherwise a lovely game.  I'm not, so for me that only saving grace is legacy version of the game under Betas.

review: Un concept magnifique mais gâché par une optimisation désastreuse (30 FPS sur un PC haut de gamme) et un gameplay beaucoup trop répétitif. Si la construction est riche et plaisante, le côté survie est une corvée : le nettoyage des îles est interminable pour des récompenses dérisoires, et le craft est freiné par des ressources inutilement rares comme la pierre dure ou le charbon. L'ergonomie est à revoir totalement : il y a trop d'établis et de coffres spécifiques, et devoir rester appuyé sur E pour chaque interaction devient vite épuisant. Le combat manque de profondeur, le système de navigation est mal équilibré et l'absence de besoins vitaux (faim/soif) rend la nourriture et l'agriculture peu utiles. En résumé, le jeu a un énorme potentiel visuel, mais il sacrifie le plaisir du joueur au profit d'un "grind" artificiel et d'une gestion d'inventaire pénible.

review:
Glider controls make the game tedious and make flying from one island to another a nightmare. Game doesn't seem to have much in the way of tutorials, so they let you run around blind and hope you figure things out. Crafting system isn't very polished, messy compared to other survival crafters on the market. Animation for gathering seems permanently lagged. Gathering resources should be smooth and quick to feel progression. But in Aloft it's slow, you can't speed it up by clicking multiple times. 

The island idea of driving your island around to explore new ones is interesting and could be something to keep working on, but they would need to overhaul the game mechanics to keep on par with it's competitors. As it stands now, it's going in the refund bin.

review:
[h1]Unplayable[/h1]
[h2]Performance issues[/h2]
Frame stutters constantly, and occasionally shows black frames(!) which other 
people are also experiencing. The performance issues have been complained about for years on the forums and it appears the devs haven't solved it yet.

[h2]Boring[/h2]
The game is very linear despite looking like an open world game. Collect resources, find the tech tree point, fight easy mobs, build, craft, repeat over and over. Everything is gated one tech tree item at a time. No sense of agency, and it ruins the exploration when it's all mandatory and prescriptive.

[h2]Annoying[/h2]
The flying is annoying. The glider always droops down when flying. In order to fly level you end up playing Angry Birds, constantly having to pull up every second. Aggravating. The third person camera also lags behind so you're fighting the camera at the same time.

[h2]Navigation[/h2]
All the islands look the same to each other, there's no compass or map (except one in your base), so it's difficult to tell where you've been and where you need to go next. It's also easy to get lost on an island since it all looks the same.

I would refund the game but I'm past the 2 hours.

review: After only a short time I felt like I was doing no deduckting but only, to steal another review's terms, throwing darts in the dark. Instead of searching for hidden clues and piecing them together to solve a mystery, you are shown everything you can interact with and given a load of words to fill in the notes in your journal then you mess about putting the words in different orders until you are told you have the right answers - no deduckting, no fail states, just trial and error with information you did no work to acquire. I get that this is a short, casual, cutesy game that's more easy-playing than brain-teaser by design, and if that's what you want then cool, but for anyone who actually wants to work things out for themselves instead of tediously trying word combos until you get the right one and can listen to a few more sentences of dialogue, this is not the game for you.

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
Played it twice a year apart in case my initial judgment was too harsh. The game costs as much as any small detective game but plays like a demo. Game's too short (~2 hours) and tutorial-level easy (on the "detective mode"; I haven't tried the "story mode" that is supposed to be even easier). The comedy-noir style is charming in the opening scene; after that, it devolves into simple duck puns.
The biggest disappointment for me was how the game handled [spoiler] Boris Petrovic, the buffalo [/spoiler]. This game uses character names as a shorthand for their personalities. For example, we meet a stern boss called [spoiler] Ernst like the German for serious [/spoiler], a frustrated customer service agent called [spoiler] Angst [/spoiler]. Even the location, Salsiccia, where [spoiler] sausages get smuggled from [/spoiler] translates to [spoiler] sausage in Italian [/spoiler]. 
If that is the case, what does the game indicate through [spoiler] Petrovic's [/spoiler] name? Etymologically, this name stems from the ancient Greek [spoiler] petros (rock), with Petrovic meaning "son of Peter" [/spoiler]. However, the character is not "stoic" at all. Instead he is an [spoiler] easily manipulated bus-driver-turned-smuggler [/spoiler]. 
I don't know how much agency was granted to the voice actor Cyrus Nemati (whose work in Hades I otherwise admire) but it does not help that [spoiler] Petrovic [/spoiler] speaks with a Hollywood-style [spoiler] non-distinct Slav [/spoiler] accent.
With all the creative freedom a duck doing detective work in a fictional world would allow, I wish there was care taken not to perpetuate stereotypes of [spoiler] Eastern European men as "dim-witted criminals" [/spoiler].

review:
The game itself is well put together. I didn’t encounter any bugs, the mechanics make sense, and the art style is cute. 

My two main qualms:

1. It’s too short.

2. There is no real satisfaction to be had in figuring something out.

I honestly thought the first case would be the first of like, three or something. Nope. It wasn’t, but I could at least live with that if I was emotionally invested in the story and/or the characters, but… Nope. There really wasn’t enough time to get to know any of them, and while some of the surface level details are cute, I wouldn’t be able to say I had a favourite, or that I ultimately cared what happened to anybody. The case was pretty straightforward, and if I ever got stuck, I found I could just jam random words into the blanks until something fit, more often than not. And like I mentioned prior, there was no real satisfaction in figuring out anything - no major plot twists, no big new location that opens up for exploration… nothing. 

It could be that I was looking for something a little more meaty and harrowing, like Obra Dinn or Roottrees, and what I ended up with was the cosy version of that, which was a little too cosy for my tastes. I guess I wanted something more challenging that lasted longer than what I got here. 

It’s not like it’s a bad game, and if you know it’s short and sweet and generally simple with zero replayability going in - and you’re able to get it on sale - more power to you. I love ducks, and I love detectives - but Duck Detective just wasn’t for me.

name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

review:
Duck Detective: The Secret Salami is supposedly an investigation-style puzzle game in the same vein as Return of the Obra Dinn or The Case of the Golden Idol. I love this genre, but unfortunately had a lousy time with Duck Detective. A good deduction puzzler gives you 2+ clues for every piece of info you're meant to logically deduce, and makes the truth logically overdetermined and watertight such that no other answer is plausible or possible. Here you get more like two thirds of a clue per piece of info, and are expected to solve the puzzles via leaps of logic or outright guesswork. (I even checked the walkthrough to see if I missed any vital clues, but I rarely did; the deductions really were meant to be that obtuse and uncompelling.) Needless to say, that made for a truly terrible gameplay experience.

Not at all recommended.
name: Duck Detective: The Secret Salami

Took me around 2 hours to do (had it idling for a bit) and while I don't necessarily mind short games this is just too much. I expected maybe a couple cases or something but I was quite shocked that it was over.

The art, voice acting, and what is here is well presented and well done. I said I don't recommend this but that's at this price point - I simply feel like I've gotten better value from other games at similar price or even lower. If it's on sale then it could be a decent evening.

review:
The parts that make up Farm Simulator are all quite good. The physics works well, the terrain works well, it's reasonably stable, visually well done, the map design is good, the tree cutting is probably the best in any game.

So why a negative review? As a game, it's very shallow and simple. There are only so many time's you're going to enjoy harvesting a field yourself. There's AI but they don't work particularly well, or at all for some tasks. This game sort of want's to be a management game I think, but it's not. Sid Meyer once said that a game is a series of interesting decisions, but there are almost no decisions in this game, there's a pretty obvious best way to do things and nothing ever changes.

It really boils down to a handful of well done minigames that become tedious after very little time. The bones are good, this could become a good game, but it's just not yet.

review:
Decided to get into agriculture, you know. Bought a tractor, bought a water tank, thought I'd nobly water my greenhouse. I pull up. And what do you think? A single, eldritch birch tree blocks my path, and my water tank gets so hopelessly stuck on it that the laws of physics completely cease to matter.

Thought I could drive around it? No, fences and collision boxes are so tight you can't get through. Fine, I'm a modern farmer, the game has a chainsaw! I bought a chainsaw. I took it out. I'm standing in front of the tree, pressing every button on my keyboard. The chainsaw won't "rev," no gas is given, no red cutting line appears—my character just blankly stares at the trunk. I tried to push the tank manually—my farmer literally headbutts it and stands there like a post, as if it's not a trailer, but a monolith from 2001: A Space Odyssey.

The game completely fails to explain basic things to a newcomer. No proper tutorial, no hints whatsoever when you get terminally stuck on flat ground. Instead of a relaxing, meditative farm sim, you get a simulator of fighting bugs, collision meshes, and the chainsaw UI.

All in all, if you want to spend two hours raging over a tree and searching the internet for the exact key combination to start a chainsaw, game of the year. To everyone else—strictly do not recommend until patches or a proper onboarding system.

review:
I honestly lost all motivation to play after the latest update.

I have spent a huge amount of time building and customizing my farm on an existing save. After the update, trees that I had previously removed suddenly came back.

And they didn’t just appear somewhere harmless. They spawned inside my cow barn, garages, factories, silos and other buildings. Some of them are literally impossible to remove because the building completely covers the tree, so I can’t even target it with an object-removal mod.

What am I supposed to do now? Demolish an expensive factory, remove the tree, and build the factory again? And repeat that everywhere this happened?

This is a farming game where players can spend hundreds of hours developing a single save. An update should NEVER restore map objects that a player deliberately removed and place them through buildings and other objects created later.

I had literally just finished developing my farm, and instead of enjoying it, I’m now expected to spend my time and in-game money cleaning up damage caused by an update.

Yes, I could demolish buildings, remove the trees and rebuild everything. But that’s not the point. I shouldn’t have to repair my save because an update broke it.

Right now, opening the game feels like starting over rather than continuing the farm I’ve spent so much time building.

Please fix this and, more importantly, provide a way to remove the incorrectly restored trees from existing saves without forcing players to demolish their buildings.

Until this is fixed, I genuinely don’t feel like playing anymore.

review:
Total waste of money. All of the mechanics available seem unfinished and delivered "in a rush", which is sarcastically impressive given that it's the nth title under the FS brand. To summarize:

1. AI workers can't get the job done on fields with irregular shapes. Also, forget about getting their help when there is a fence or a tree nearby. At least the game tells you that they're stuck... oh wait, it doesn't; they'll just keep climbing the tree;
2. You are paying one-third of an AAA game's cost for almost no content. Unless you belong to this entire "realism!!!111!one!!" Ursus-lovers cult, you'd be surprised that such a title has relied on and invested in the same crops since the first released version and still gets as many positive reviews. Sugar cane? Rice? Grapes? You'd better stick with the one and only vehicle in the original game...
3. ...unless you want to dive into the modding community guarded by all these old-equipment fanatics. At least they do the work that should have been done by the studio itself. The developers genuinely sell you just a platform with a faulty engine full of bugs.
4. It would be fair if they argued against the above, but they consciously added the "reset vehicle" function to the base game, knowing that in a lot of scenarios your equipment just... breaks without any specific reason.
5. Did I mention they promise you realism? Sure, unless you check the prices and the value you get from the corresponding equipment. You'd better save money to afford the potato planter with all of its modern features that simply do not exist in the game.
6. You're saving for the aforementioned planter, so you don't want to waste money on a better tractor? It's fine, just accept any contract and use the borrowed vehicle forever. Sure, you won't be able to use the attached equipment, but you can always attach yours.
7. Feed the animals; otherwise, they won't survive. Just kidding, they can be kept with 0% health for ages without any consequences. You call that family friendly? Is keeping the animals hungry yet alive giving a good example of how to care for living creatures?
8. Cultivate, seed, fertilize, roll and use the weeder (in that order - yes, you can use the weeder when nothing has risen from the ground yet) in the same month, and you'll be golden. Full immersion, except not.
9. Tired of realism? Take loans. Lots of loans. The interest rates are piffling.

I could spend a few hours listing all the things that make the price even more unreasonable, but it all boils down to one expression (you can call it a warning if you want) - the developers should cowboy up, start treating the player base seriously, and invest in QA. You're lying to people and the gamers are not stupid. They notice.

review:
[h1]Farming Simulator 25[/h1]
[b]Excellent visuals, but I recommend waiting for a sale.[/b]
[i]Updated September 9, 2026. Written as an FS22 player, FS25 server renter, and someone with small-farm and livestock experience.[/i]

[h1]The Good[/h1]

[b]Pumps N' Hoses is finally here[/b]
The free Pumps N' Hoses Pack launched on September 8, developed by Creative Mesh and published by GIANTS. This is exactly the kind of farming-focused addition I welcome. I hope returning content continues to be improved and expanded, not simply brought across from FS22 and left there.

[b]Excellent graphics and ground deformation[/b]
The detailed graphics look fantastic. Visually, I have little to complain about.

Ground deformation is a genuine improvement. Tires leaving ruts and reacting to softer ground make fieldwork feel more physical. I like how vehicles affect the ground, even though the separate landscaping tool still needs work.

[h1]The Mixed: Not Entirely Good or Bad[/h1]

[b]Familiar gameplay, but familiar limitations[/b]
Coming from FS22, the familiar experience makes it easy to settle in. However, some areas feel more like a continuation than a meaningful upgrade.

To my ears, the standard sound design feels familiar too. I have not noticed the same leap in audio that I see in the graphics.

[b]A good animal selection, but limited involvement[/b]
I enjoy the variety of livestock, but animal farming should involve more than supplying resources and waiting for products.

I grew up watching my father shear sheep and have raised chickens myself, so the simplified care routines stand out to me.

[b]Reasons for cautious optimism[/b]
Beans & Alpacas, scheduled for October 27, 2026, promises manual shearing or hiring a worker. That is exactly the kind of choice I want.

I want that approach extended to existing livestock, especially sheep. I hope GIANTS is adapting, but I am not putting all my eggs in one basket.

[h1]The Bad: Areas That Need Improvement[/h1]

[b]Animal care needs substantially more depth[/b]
Chickens are my clearest example: the standard care system requires feeding but no water-refilling task. Having raised chickens, I find that disappointing. A basic water-care option should be a free improvement, not paid DLC.

I also want bedding replacement, coop cleaning, day-and-night routines, and optional illness and flock-health management. Caring for animals should mean more than filling a resource meter.

Breeding could involve rams for sheep and a meaningful rooster role in producing chicks. Hens do not need a rooster to lay ordinary eggs, but breeding chicks is different. I also want to raise young male chicks, not just buy adult roosters.

Sheep should offer manual shearing or hiring a shearer. That should not be an interaction reserved for a different animal in an expansion.

I want deeper links between soil condition, crop and feed quality, storage, pests, and animal health. Advanced systems could be optional. I would consider an animal-care expansion, but basic care should not require another purchase.

[b]Repairs should involve more than a menu[/b]
The repair experience still feels too familiar to me. I would like to open the hood, inspect components, identify a problem, order parts through a farmhouse computer, and use the appropriate tools to fix it.

Filters, batteries, belts, brakes, hydraulics, and damaged header teeth could provide practical tasks. Repair skills could improve with experience. Players wanting convenience could pay a mechanic or request vehicle collection and delivery.

Cleaning and maintenance could affect component wear and metal corrosion more meaningfully, creating practical work and a foundation modders could expand.

[b]Landscaping, roads, and fences need better tools[/b]
The landscaping interface still feels too close to the FS22 experience. I want more precise controls and an easier way to browse and apply modded ground, yard, and road textures through clearly organized categories.

A connected road tool would help: place control points, adjust curves and heights, and let the road follow or shape the terrain. Fences also need smoother placement and alignment. Building a farm should feel creative, not awkward.

[b]Forestry needs a more noticeable step forward[/b]
Logging and chainsaw audio feel very familiar. I wanted better handling and more interaction, not simply more equipment.

I would welcome optional tree regeneration, including a simplified setting where retaining a stump allows regrowth and removing it prevents that regrowth. This would not need to apply to every species. Server owners should be able to disable it.

[b]Weather should interact more convincingly with vehicles[/b]
I have noticed rain audio that makes it sound as though rain is hitting the vehicle even when it is sheltered inside a building. That breaks the immersion.

I want more convincing rain and snow effects on windows, with water running across the glass and wipers making a practical difference to visibility.

[b]The server-management interface feels outdated[/b]
As a paying server renter, the web panel I use is a frustration. I have not found convenient mod-name searching, useful active/inactive filters, or straightforward bulk selection and removal.

Managing many mods should not require so much manual searching. Removing selected mods or clearing the collection should be straightforward without risking the savegame.

This describes the panel I use, not every hosting provider.

[b]Mod support and content priorities concern me[/b]
Modders add enormous value, but the variety available for my interests has grown more slowly than I hoped. I have heard complaints about restrictive approvals, but cannot verify individual cases or blame every delay on GIANTS.

Quality testing matters, especially in multiplayer. I would like a clearer, efficient approval process that supports creative mods without unnecessary restrictions.

The free Emergency Pack from Creative Mesh, published by GIANTS, is not content I personally want on my server. Rural emergencies have a place, but firefighting is not my priority in a farming game. I would rather see more depth in everyday farm work.

[b]Smaller farms deserve more attention[/b]
My experience included a small John Deere used for mowing and pulling a wagon, not a fleet of expensive commercial machinery. I want more emphasis on that starting point: compact equipment, hand tools, small trailers, and practical small-farm jobs.

Small tractors exist, but I want stronger gameplay around them and progression toward larger operations.

[b]More optional multiplayer systems would help[/b]
I would like a built-in way to list and sell an entire farm to another player, not just manage individual land purchases. Player-run stalls where people buy and sell goods would also make a server feel more connected.

Optional hunger, thirst, fatigue, and workplace injuries could add depth to realism-focused servers. Owners should control these settings and recovery times, with everything switchable off.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]

[b]Worth considering at a discount, but not worth full price to me right now.[/b]

FS25 has strengths, and Pumps N' Hoses is a positive step. However, too much still feels like FS22 with improvements around it, not the deeper farming simulator I hoped for.

I want more attention given to existing systems before the focus moves to the next addition. Farming should feel like more than operating increasingly large equipment.

Before buying, watch an ongoing YouTube series from someone who plays regularly. Look beyond trailers and opening episodes, and check which features come from the base game, DLC, or mods.

[b]Overall, it is a decent game with potential, but it still needs substantial improvement. Do your research and buy it on sale.[/b]

review:
Been a long time fan of the Series way before I even knew about Steam and I really do want to like this game. There are some nice features in it like the introduction of somewhat deformable terrain after the community asked for it for the past decade. However there are so many other parts of the game that are simply not enjoyable (Physics, Missions which break frequently, Basic features missing like searchable controls, no Shop search and many more). The most important thing to me tho is the performance (or the lack of it): I simply cannot get over the simply dreadful job the developers have done at trying to get this game to run on anything other than a single core CPU running at at least 6 GHz. A game that still only utilizes one core being released in 2024 is wild stuff, since the last single core chip came out in 2013.
I can get over the shader compilation making the game stutter initially despite me preferring a loading bar, I can also get over map loading times being somewhat long which can be somewhat remedied by using a fast drive, but getting 25FPS with a PC that is capable of running pretty much anything you throw at it simply because I'm mowing grass or harvesting a crop (Both core gameplay features btw.)? I know 180FPS is not needed for a farming game, but having choppy frame times with drops from 90 to 25FPS makes gameplay simply really difficult to enjoy.
Recently the game also decided that it needed to leak memory for whatever reason which ends in it freezing after some playtime and never recovering. Reinstalling the game and disabling all mods also did not help.

TLDR:
I don't know what kind of priorities management has, but I will stay far away from this series until either the engine improves or gets changed out for something that's not straight out of 1995. I will not even talk about features and improvements since those are already mostly being propped up by the modding community.
I really hoping Saber's upcoming farming game will offer what I'm looking for. For the time being I will most likely resort to earlier entries which were at least still playable

[b]TL;DR:[/b] Great mods. Little to no technical progress. Greedy DLC policy. More and more content is being locked behind overpriced paywalls.

[hr]

FS25 can still be a fun game, mainly because of its incredible modding community. Ironically, the community often delivers better content than the developers themselves.

Unfortunately, there is barely any technical progress compared to previous Farming Simulator titles. With every new release, innovation seems to slow down even further.

The DLC policy is the biggest problem. Gameplay mechanics that should be part of the base game are increasingly being sold as expensive DLCs. Many paid vehicles already existed as free, higher-quality mods long before they were added to overpriced Season Passes.

Less than two years after release, you're looking at around €30 for the base game, ~€75 for the Season Passes, or ~€110 if you buy every DLC individually. To make matters worse, it feels like content was cut from the base game before launch just so it could be sold later as DLC.

GIANTS Software seems more interested in maximizing short-term profits than building a better game or maintaining its reputation.

I genuinely hope a serious competitor enters this niche. Farming Simulator has needed competition for years, and players deserve better.

review:
This is the only real farming sim on the market.  That should be the review in and of itself.  But it isn't.

A few good things first before I bash this for what it's worth:
- A ton of articulation.  You really don't know detail until you pay attention to the equipment in this game.
- Equipment variation is paramount here.  Many different manufacturers and multiple different ways to accomplish the same goal.
-Mods are really what carries the game in general.  If it weren't for these kind souls, this would be in the dollar bin.

Now on to everything bad:

-No new engine.  It is no different than how Bethesda releases games.  They 'overhaul' their engine, in this case the GIANTS engine, and over time, since 2009, it gets more and more bloated and bugs from years ago still continue to exist.  It's like painting layer after layer over a turd and then wondering why it not only looks like a painted turd but rolls off the wall as such.  I've heard fanboy after fanboy say it isn't possible-- it's probably not possible given that every equipment manufacturer is lining their pockets and it's the only farming sim out there.  Money speaks volumes.  It isn't possible to do exactly all of this on a new engine or even an existing one?  Or is it your pride?
- No multicore support.  I've heard varying different accounts but the overwhelming seem to be one core, one thread.  Impressive in 2009.  Not impressive when you have this much going on, on any CPU.  I mean, my GPU usage hangs between 50 and 60 percent because there simply isn't any more my poor, poor core can give.  For a game that looks this bad, I shouldn't be getting only a hundred FPS with stuttering on a 4090 at 4k with a 13900K.  And from what I hear, from an ex employee, they will not be changing this any time soon.  One core, one thread, maxed out and nothing else.  Literally 6 percent.
- The graphics.  Look, it still looks like it's from 2009 but with some effects slathered over it.  Great.  Would be tolerable and nice if it performed well.  Granted, I understand how complex it is to process some of this stuff.
- The DLC.  What is with this fire emergency pack?  What does that have to do with the side of farming the playerbase is interested in?  Granted it's free, but it's terrible.  And ground deformation in a paid DLC?  No, let's not focus on the glaring issues at hand, here's another piece of equipment you can't afford until you're making so much money that it doesn't matter what you use.  How sad is it that you can't even be bothered to look even in the mods section and see what needs to be fixed?
- Reliance on mods.  Now there is some debate with this.  No problem at all with using different equipment from mods, it's hard to program in a million variations just because a farmer at home actually owns a specific tractor.  But for it to actually be semi realistic and tolerable, you NEED to use mods.  From the tines sinking into the ground to accurate dirt colors, to how mud forms when it rains, it isn't optional.  Any game that I have ever played that relies on mods this much, simply isn't good.  Mods should be optional and not needed for a well rounded game.
-Everything other than equipment and the fields is simply an afterthought.  Standard affair here for any of these 'simulator' games.  One old dude at the base farm simply rotates on an axis, staring at you like you punched his wife.  No attention to much else other than the equipment.  Traffic is terrible.  Detail on buildings is terrible.  But it is a farming game after all.  I reckon you can't have everything.
- The price.  Like I said with every previous point, it's like a 30 dollar game at best and the DLC should be free.  You want big money?  How about making a big money game?  Or are you more focused on your new racing game when you can't even get a farming game right?

I could go on and on and on.  But I won't.  This is the only game for a farming fix if you aren't a real farmer.  I will continue to play it because I paid for it.  But I should have my head checked for believing anything had changed when it released.  If you aren't into farming at a hardcore level, just go away and play Stardew Valley.  It's far superior in every single way.

Instead of improving the core mechanics, which have been lagging for the 10 years I've been playing, they just keep releasing the same unoptimized slop packaged with a few unnecessary gimmick features.

The farming simulator genre desperately needs some real competition. We almost had it with Cattle & Crops, which was a promising game before it was abandoned. Until another developer steps up to challenge them, Giants has no incentive to actually fix their game.

Any engine in 2026 that [b]uses only one core for all computing[/b] purposes in the game is absolutely pathetic and lazy. The only reason this game is giving you performance issues is that the whole damn [b]90% of your CPU is relaxing[/b] while the only remaining thread is being choked by an ancient engine that belongs to 2008.

(Old Review): I am recommending this game with one major warning. THIS GAME HAS ISSUES. Buy it only if you are okay with dealing with some issues. 

I have been playing farming simulator since FS19 and have logged many hours across the games leading up to this one and have logged a fair share of hours on this game (more on console) and I believe I have come up with a solid opinion. First and foremost, this game has issues, there is no denying that. The worst offenders are poor optimization and graphics rendering, this game runs poorly unless you have a fairly high end machine (I do not), with frequent lag spikes and graphical glitches. While help is available from the community most issues cannot be fixed by yourself, leaving many players begging for help from GIANTS to fix bugs that they don't seem interested in fixing. 

The other massive issue is a personal one. GIANTS, in my opinion released this game too soon after the previous game and in doing so massively damaged the modding community, in my time playing this game it feels like the modding community has shrunk with several notable modders seemingly vanishing even though they regularly uploaded mods on pervious games, I am unsure if this is simply the modders losing interest or if it is the modders feeling as if their work is being thrown away by frequent releases leaving their hard work behind. Either way, as I said on a personal level I feel GIANTS is responsible. 

Now, all of that aside this game is fun, it does some things and added some things that previous titles were missing. I do enjoy playing this game, despite its issues, which is why I am comfortable recommending it. Farming Simulator has taught me more about farming and the way our world works in a few years than school ever did. And lets be honest, there is something incredibly satisfying about building an efficient farm.

I recommend this game only to those willing to deal with its issues, however, I cannot recommend the franchise itself enough, if you are unwilling to deal with FS25's issues check out the previous games, especially if those games still have working mod hubs or modding communities, FS only gets better with mods. review:
This franchise hasn't had truly meaningful improvements to its engine in, oh, about a decade. Sure they added parallax, but act like it's Snowrunner levels of terrain deformation. Yeah, they added seasons, but somehow made it worse than the mod they ripped it from. They added fog, improved textures, and slightly better lighting, which, you know what, it does look good alongside some better color balancing. That's honestly all I can think of off the top of my head though. They keep making the engine version number go up, but not much else changes besides that.

 No major physics updates (no matter how much they say there were), Ai is still braindead, crops and textures still instantly change instead of smoothly transitioning, vehicles move around and act like weightless toys, contracts are bugged beyond belief, Features such as more in depth animal husbandry or vehicle maintenance/controls have been requested for years yet are ignored... I could go on.

But hey, for $60, you get a completely "new" title! we added rice and a few new tractors! I've got a new pair of keys to jingle in front of you! More equipment packs for an extra $10 no one asked for too! You know what though, at least they were making improvements, even if minimal, and bundling it all in one game. Better than them making fundamental improvements and paywalling it behind DLC.

Oh wait, that's exactly what they are doing now.

Yeah, their latest DLC, The SKY Agriculture pack, adds such niche equipment no one normally uses such as; cultivators, seeders, sprayers and spreaders, and rollers. you know, things that really warrant being their own content. The real kicker though? The DLC also comes with improved equipment physics, better animations, as well as dirt accumulation (not just a different texture) and terrain deformation changes. Why these things couldn't have been added to all equipment and pushed as a major update is beyond me. But I guess why would they do that when they can just make a handful of bug fixes and another frontloader arm, label that as an update, and call it a day

review:
I don’t want to be a pure hater of FS25. Game has enough new content and visible improvements to feel like a new entry: GPS, better atmosphere, volumetric sky/fog, terrain deformation, etc.

But the priorities feel strange. Problems have been screaming for several games already, and they still feel more important than “wow, Japan map.”

Biggest disappointment is terrain and mud physics. Yes, deformation exists, but it feels more like a visual tire path pushed into the ground than a real soil/mud system. I didnt expect SnowRunner, but I expected the ground to feel more alive and vehicles to interact with it more naturally.

Graphics are also inconsistent. Game looks nice in ~60% of playtime, especially with fog and lighting, but then terrain materials and normal maps change right in front of you. Sky is "volumetric", but often still feels like a noisy flat layer. Vehicles can look strangely flat too, with weak AO/contact shadows, so they dont always feel properly grounded.

[b]The economy has the usual FS problem too: Poor field/crop farmers suffer, greenhouse landlords know peace. [/b]

FS25 is not a bad game. The core loop is still addictive, fans of the series will probably enjoy it. But many core systems still feel old or half modernized. It feels like GIANTS added good new content, but avoided fixing some deeper problems that have been there for years.

Recommended only if you already like fs and know what youre getting
Tutorial is still basically "press WASD to walk"...

review:
I wanted to love this game, but I simply can't. The concept is amazing, and I quite enjoyed it when it worked. Unfortunately, the amount of negative aspects well overwhelmed the positive aspects of the game. 

Some of the problems are plain bugs. The contract system was total garbage. New contracts stopped spawning, only contracts of certain types were spawning. The AI was garbage. Sometimes it just couldn't figure out how to get unblocked, simple tasks took way longer than it ought to have, and it made bizarre choices. Deadwood contracts were frustrating, because sometimes the target trees spawned INSIDE other trees, meaning you had to cut down the wrong tree to get to it, but cutting down the wrong tree meant you got a penalty larger than the contract amount! Picking up tree branches was super buggy, frequently dropping them, and having them get stuck in the wood chipper.

Most of the problems however, are just inexplicably bad design. Certain features of some vehicles which cost money were purely decorative, with no indication of that, such as the tow hitch on the ATV. Harvesting root crops solo was virtually impossible. The carrot harvesting machine, for instance, had no storage, so you had to assign that to an AI, which you then had to drive alongside to catch the harvest from. However, since the AI was so bad, it made doing that the most frustrating thing ever! Forestry contracts were equally bad. They couldn't be assigned to an AI, so you had to do those manually, and the ratio of pay per time spend was abysmal!

Ultimately, I had to stop playing, because contracts simply wouldn't respawn, no matter what I did. No amount of waiting, sleeping, using (or not using) mods could fix it. I moved to a new map, but then i lost 45 minutes of progress because the game crashed. Mega frustrating.

The good parts were really good, and I hate that I can't recommend this, but the bad parts were just so bad, so frequent, and so unpredictable, that I just have to say, you should probably stay away from this game. I'm not sure I'll ever buy another GIANTS game either, this experience has just left such a bad taste in my mouth. Bugs aside, it feels like they haven't even bothered to play the game to make sure it works and is fun, and the bugs on top just make it even more unplayable.

review:
This game is a cash grab. It's mostly a reskin of FS22 with DLC that seems to be directly developed from mod assets that were stolen from the modding community. Which, I didn't play FS22 so I didn't realize this until digging deeper into the community. But honestly, even outside of that issue, it's tedious in so many ways. For example, the tutorial doesn't show you how to do hardly anything; you HAVE to watch youtube tutorial videos to learn how to do almost al the tasks / how to use 95% of the equipment. 

A lot of the gameplay and equipment is realistic in bad ways, i.e. it feels grindy and cumbersome to drive. Some of the equipment, like the Dewulf ZKIVSE Harvester, is bugged to hell. You literally cannot use it in 1-player mode because you need to drive the container for holding the produce right next to it the whole time you're driving it or else it will dump all your harvest everywhere - in other words, you need another person who is perfectly synced up with your driving - and the AI for that task is also bugged to hell so you need a real person. I didn't figure this out until I spent 3 HOURS harvesting a beet field. It was such a grind and by the end, I had to cancel the contract because I didn't realize 99% of the beets I harvested were just all over the field, with no way to pick them up and turn them in. So when I canceled the contract, it paid me -$135,000, putting my net worth in the negative and requiring me to use a money cheat to undo. Another player had reported this problem on the official Giants forum in Fall 2024 and Giants (the makers of FS25) removed their comment instead of resolving it. A year and a half later, this crucial early contract is still totally non-functional. In fact, I had to use a money cheat twice to make this game playable. Wtf.

I bought this game on sale but if I knew what a grind it would be, and how immersion-breaking it would be to attempt to complete the contracts & have to salvage my save with cheats, I wouldn't have bought it at all. Don't bother. Go spend your money on a game made by a company who cares about product quality rather than producing iterations of the same game repeatedly with minimal improvements between each one. The more I look into them, the more Giants feels like a scummy company to me, a symbol of some of the main things wrong with the video game industry and our world at large. 3/10.

review: I have put a lot of hours in on this game. It was supposed to be something low intensity that I could have running in the background while I did my office work, taking short breaks to get things on track to run while I got back to work. The game has proven to be a headache. I found myself running on the hamster wheel of work arounds and trouble shooting. In fact I can't think of a single session I've run with the game where everything has gone smoothly; production facilities mysteriously stop producing after running perfectly for a few months of game time. AI mysteriously can't find its way to and from destinations, runs itself into buildings, spins in endless circles or decides not to recognize that the crop in the field is ready to harvest despite having the proper equipment. Need to level some ground to build a factory? Good luck with that, you'll get half way through the project only to find that the leveling function stops working so you're left with the choice of finding an absolutely flat piece of ground, placing the building anyway so one end floats while the other clips into the ground or abandon the project completely. I had to give up on the idea of forestry because none of the controls for the timber harvesters worked. Mods to help with some of these issues? Yup, but then they often cause more conflict. With all the issues that I ran into with the the glitches, crashes, physics conflicts etc... it felt like I had taken on another job instead of playing a game. I hope someday to be able to come back to FS25 but it seems like there is a whole lot that Giant needs to get figured out before this game lives up to the huge potential it has.

I'm conflicted. I find myself spending hours on end on it, just like I did with Farming Simulator 22. And I'm geniunely enjoying it. If you don't have any of the previous Farming Simulator titles, go for it. If you have one of the previous ones, there is very little need to upgrade. It's almost exactly the same as before. It's addictive and enjoyable, but at the same time it has things that are absolutely infuriating.

Things that are bad:
* Handeling anything with anything. Moving pallets, Logging with the truck or even worse, the big grabby-grabby CAT machine... Things fly everywhere and is not natural at all.... Was exactly the same in 22, and I have heard exactly the same as 19....
* The traffic AI is absolutely horrendus. Impossible to play with it on. It could just as well have been left out of the game. And what the hell is that school bus doing driving around in the middle of the night... Creepy stuff...
* The AI for doing things on the farm feels only half way done. If that. 
* * It can harvest, but lets the auger out into the field every other row. Causing you to ruin your crops if you drive on it. 
* * It can't pick up bales, bale bales or wrap bales. I mean. Com'on. That should be incredibly easy. 
* * It can skip every other row, but can't have two AI's working on the same field with the same gear. One example of this is giant fields when gathering rocks. 
* * Can not use AI to empty out harvesters or any machine that otherwise will just stop and wait for you to do things. This forces you into the least intersting part of the operation. You are basically the bus-boy for the AI. Great.
* * If you want to harvest potatoes you can't get the AI to follow you, you have to follow it, and it does not care about you at all. Driving into you at any chance it gets. 

And there is so many more things that are just... frustrating...

Generally the idea of a farming simulator is amazing. I love it, but for some reason the creators keep reinventing the wheel, focusing on things that look good, but forget to make the gameplay smooth. It's a 50-50 super frustrating and blissful experience.... 

Playing it makes me think that they need a competitor. Someone to make them focus on the quality of the game, instead of just recreating it and releasing it again...

Oh and.. more vehicles this time, but removed a bunch of vehicles from FS22... why.... just... 'sigh'.. just create one version of the game. Improve it, add DLC's and make it into a gem, instead of a half polished turd that gets re-wrapped every other year...

review:
The lack of comprehensive tutorial made this game virtually unplayable. I should not have to seek out more information online to figure out how to play your game. 

The tutorial takes about 30 minutes and is only teaches you how to use three/four different equipment types, how to prepare your field, seed, and harvest..... that's it. It does not tell you how to purchase/use more equipment, seeds, animals, etc. and does not indicate what you are to do to start your farm. At minimum, the in-game tutorial should show me 95% of how to play the game. The current tutorial probably shows about 10% of what you need to know to begin and maintain your farm. It also does not seem to provide any further information on game play post tutorial as there are minimal "objectives" that you can do. Even if you select one of the available "objectives", it does not tell you what you need to do, it just marks a random farm on your map. Also, you can "rent" equipment, but when I selected that option, the equipment was nowhere to be found. I checked all over my farm and the farm indicated on the map, but I could not find anything.

I have played many games similar to this so I do not need my hand held, but this was the worst tutorial process on a game I have ever encountered. Unless you are very familiar with the franchise or the tutorial is completely overhauled and made better, I would not recommend wasting your money.

I'm really trying to get into the game and try it, but damn does it eat up your limited refund window with wild nonsense:
- Laggy on a 9070xt, good luck finding the culprit in the dozens of graphics settings
- Long shader rendering time
- Missing 1920x1200 resolution
- game.xml changes don't always propagate to the runtime
- "Invert Y" affects both keyboard and mouse
- "Invert Y" doesn't work inside vehicles
- Steam controller override for "invert Y" doesn't work inside vehicles
- Mouse isn't captured by the game window
- You can't manually pick gamepad bindings, which is a pain for setting stick axes
- You have to temporarily increase your stick deadzones to change controller axes (otherwise look-up/look-down/etc will get mapped to both X and Y axes at the same time)
- Missing sensitivity curves for gamepad sticks, triggers
- Missing outer deadzones for gamepad sticks
- InputBinding.xml duplicates gamepad entries over and over again...
- editing gameSettings.xml has no effect on the game
- Game spends a minute phoning home on every startup


Cool cool. 97 minutes in and I've finally fixed the damn controls so that the mouse stays normal and the gamepad is fully inverted:
- in game, turn Invert-Y off
- Steam controller remap, turn right-stick Invert-Y on
- in game, delete both "player" and "vehicle" look-up and look-down entries for the gamepad
- in game, add ONLY ONE of either look-up or look-down to the game pad controls (the other is automatically mapped to the opposite)

Finally. _Now_ I can actually try playing this game. Maybe eventually I'll have an update about the actual gameplay...

review:
❌ Not a Simulator, More Like an Arcade for Kids

I honestly don’t understand who this game is made for anymore.
Right now, it feels like a 3+ kids game, not a simulation.

There is no real difficulty, no meaningful challenge, and no reason to improve your skills. A proper Pro / Hardcore mode is badly needed if this wants to be taken seriously.

The physics are basically non-existent. You flip over, crash into objects, hit walls at full speed… and nothing happens. No damage, no consequences, no realism.
Are we really stuck with 2002-level physics in a modern simulator?

For a game that calls itself a simulation, this is unacceptable. Realistic vehicle behavior, proper physics, and actual penalties should be the foundation — not optional features.

At the moment, the game plays it extremely safe, too arcade, too shallow.

Disappointing for longtime fans of the genre.

review: I've played this game for nearly 200 hours, hoping it would start feeling more rewarding. It doesn't. In fact, the game gradually becomes more and more frustrating. You can only automate (with AI) the enjoyable tasks like weeding or spraying. The tedious, time-consuming ones—like logging or harvesting beets—are a chore and have to be done manually. The game has a ton of bugs and feels closer to an alpha build than a new installment of an established product. In many cases, you have to guess what a given action will do—for example, how far a water tank will reach next to a greenhouse, why it doesn't work for animals, or why some branches get pulled into the sawmill while others don't. The same goes for machinery—there are no clear labels, so you have to buy equipment only to find out it's incompatible with your machines or unsuitable for the task you bought it for. The user interface is simply inconvenient. It took me a week to discover that worker indicators are visible in the AI steering wheel icon on the map. Thanks, but no thanks... I prefer games where you can actually see the results of your efforts.

There is a lot of cutscnene, I can even tell you that there is too much cutscene. I can accept it if it was good for the gameplay progression or to giving context, but no. Most of it just for nonsense fanservice later. People would start bitching out saying its important for the map where connecting the dot, well I mean yes, but why do you even need that one to begin with? what is the main purpose for it in gameplay progression? Nothing, its only for story fanservice reason, and its cannot be skipped, I thought it just for people who really loves the characters but no, You HAD to know the characters, Which in my opinion, all of them is like written by far left DEI people, but that is another topic to dig into.

[h2] 2. My second biggest complaint, the good, the bad and the girl boss (the dialogues) [/h2]
God, if you hate girl boss characters, stay away from this game, because every girl in this game is a girl boss archetype lmao, even the grandma is a girl boss, every male in this game is some kind of loser spineless yesmen. Terrible, do people who made the story for this game ever met a normal woman? I had a feeling that the ones who made lines and character for this game is blue haired, piercings, fat white woman. Its just my instinct because holy sheesh, the lines is god awful. Even though I hate the personality, the god awful girlboss ish lines, I liked the character design, I think its cool and unique of each character. If only they make the characters to be likable. Making the girl bossing around and the male to be yesmen loser like MCU GoG, won't make them likable, we see that already in concord. If you going to give me the "oh its military settings so..." I get it some people liked a girl boss characters but those characters have some niche parts, some are smoking hot face, or big tits, or tsundere ish, people would love it, but no. The girl boss in this game have none of that, its just plain far left girl boss that "EVERYONE" hated.

[h2] 3. Now let's talk about the gameplay [/h2]
I liked the gameplay. NGL at some point, I think to myself, wow, this is going to be one of great niche game in my library, but then the narrative story happens. But enough talking about narrative side of it, I think if you read this far, you already know what bother me the most. The gameplay is fine, but there is not much variations or freedom even if you can have a bunch of freedom, its all actually just an illusion. The moment the tutorial never allowed you or forcing you to complete some scenarion in specific way, Even you actually accomplished it without that way, you just know, the rest of the game going to be in the same format. The freedom to do anything is just illusion, the level design is really well done I give them that. But well done in a sense where the player can only accomplished it in specific strategy. You know, this game is literally one youtube search away from completely finished the game entirely. What Im trying to say is the game is too formulaic, or ish. The game is intended to be played in specific way, yes you can do in other way as well but clearly it will never be better than the intended one. Its like people who design the game have cheatsheet. This one however, completely falls flat in comparison.

Well Im not going to nitpick even further like how the artystyle or the UI UX tho, but overall a terrible experience for me, but if Im ignoring the story and the lines, its a decent experience with sometimes, not everytime, but sometimes its fun. Im buying this game expecting something great while doubting after seeing the "overwhelmingly positive" review, and Im really liked to be proven wrong but then again. My take on this if you want to find a good dumb fun tactics game with marvel Guardian of galaxy ish type characters and jokes, this is a great game for you. but for people who looking for a great experience of gameplay and story like into the breach, this is just not it gang. review:
So this game has a problem with writing.  It is the most unfunny people in existence constantly trying to be funny, it is genuinely unbearable.  I've heard people complain about dialogue before for other games like Forspoken and I always thought "ah people are being a bit too harsh" but not here, I cannot put into words how obnoxious the writing is for this game, whoever wrote it should never be allowed to put pen to paper again.  I got through the first two acts reading everything and after that I began skipping literally everything, it's too painful to read.  THANKFULLY this game is very generous with what you're allowed to skip, you can skip all dialogue, you can skip this tedious map pinning minigame, hell you can even skip levels if you feel so inclined.  If they had just made this game purely gameplay focused with zero writing it'd be so much better.  To be fair, the hideous corporate art style should have been a dead giveaway it'd have this type of writing but I like tactics game so I figured I can ignore the art.

As for the actual gameplay, early on it's a bit odd and not great.  The problem is they make the levels into fairly simple puzzles, where it's easy to complete the level but they add optional challenge objectives like kill X enemies in a certain manner, or finish in so many turns, however these challenges are usually dependent upon you having specific upgrades unlocked that you get as you level so if you didn't take that specific upgrade you can't do the challenge and are just stuck with an easy level.  Now that's early on, the later levels tend to be better as you get more units and more abilities so you can tackle the levels in different ways and with the amounts of enemies coming in and what's going on it starts to feel more tactics focused and less like puzzles with very clear solutions.  They did a pretty good job with the abilities, I was a bit worried it'd just be like using guns except you're shooting fire and ice, but no they got creative with the various styles of magic and each unit plays completely differently.  

So overall, if you skip all of the dialogue and can push through the weak start I think you can get to a pretty fun tactics game, but this game is just weighed down so much by having to press skip so much, looking at a very uninteresting art style, and a lackluster early game it's hard to recommend.  I hope in the future the team could just focus on gameplay and grab a different artstyle, maybe make something like an Into the Breach or The Last Spell.
