review:
I have depression. Playing games is one of a few ways I try to take my mind off of things that would typically worsen that depression, something that is proving exceptionally more difficult at the time of this writing. I actively avoid media that would obviously worsen that depression. I keep up on my anti-depression meds. This is how I take care of myself.

People are free to enjoy the media that they enjoy, and some people will, and have, really enjoyed this game. I won't fault people for that. As much as I hate to say it, I think I'm probably a case study for why some things need content warnings, because I'm going to be carrying this game's ending with me now and I really wish I didn't have to carry that on top of everything else I deal with on a day-to-day basis.

That said, I will not be directly spoiling anything. I went in blind, which if you're like me, I strongly advise you not to do. Watch a playthrough, or preferably just read up on the community posts first. Those'll mostly tell you all you need to know whether this is a game you'll be able to enjoy or not.

All that aside, the investigative gameplay was great, but a little lacking. They introduce tools and mechanics you use once and never again, which feels like a lot of wasted potential.

Again, if you're like me and prefer to play games to escape having to dwell on all the problems with real life, I advise you to give this game a pass and instead, pick up Scrutinized and play it on Detective Mode. Similar gameplay without reminding you quite as much about how much you really hate some aspects of the world you live in.

I think if I weren't in the mental state I'm in, I probably would have enjoyed the game more, and even appreciated the ending more. It is certainly realistic. It wraps up exactly how I would expect this scenario to end in the real world. I think that's why I hate it. It's just reaffirmation that good things don't actually happen to good people. Something I was already well aware of, and really didn't need a reminder.

You interact with the game via a computer interface; it has a notebook a terminal and a calculator. Which you have no use for none of them. At the final act, you get to copy paste a single command per storybeat to terminal but that's really it. Whole game is point and click
name: The Operator

review:
There was a lot of effort put into this game, but I'm not quite sure if it paid off for me. The main storyline was predictable, no red herrings or distractions from this main plot. There are no consequences to any of the choices I made. Like no matter what option I picked, I was going to get the same outcome - I'd rather fail and have a rewind to try an interaction again. 

I really enjoyed some of the mechanisms that were set up - identifying cars, substances, and etc. I wish there was more of them, and a bit more substance to it rather than just clicking and having pop-ups. An example of having more substance would be if I had a car identifying task I get given a line up of cars to choose from to deduce the correct one. Or if there was a gunshot I'd have to analyse it at least a little bit, like the angle of how the shot happened could help deduce the height of the killer. But no, after I scrape the surface of a puzzle I'm pushed back into the strict dialogue. 

Some of the visuals were really silly and took me out of the immersions, [spoiler]like why was Kathrine 3ft in the hallway, and 5ft10 in the locker room[/spoiler], especially when juxtaposed to real headshots of real humans, as well as illustrations. 

As of writing this, I've completed the main storyline in 3 hours. Wasn't worth it for me.

There is absolutely no freedom, second path or any autonomy at any point - just like entering the credentials - you just need to type anything and watch the correct letters appear - so is the game deciding what you do and where you end up, the only point of failure available - a bomb defusal that you can replay and read a frustrating long manual with no back button for absolutely no plot or artistic reason over and over. There is no skipping pointless dialogue or blurred (for no reason other than lack of budget, I guess) cutscenes between the days. Overall unpleasant gameplay, unpleasant ending and most of all unpleasant waste of money to buy sheer frustration for 3 hours.

review: Don't get me wrong, it's an interesting story and the final plot twist is one I definitely didn't expect. The UI and the mechanics were interesting, and while it wasn't very hard at least I didn't have to ask for help so it's pretty easy access for people who aren't hardcore into mystery solving. However, I feel like this concept could have gone SO much further- the open ending could have allowed for at least twice as much story and overall I feel like the whole Operator thing should have lasted longer- either been stretched out more in time (because timeline wise this all happens VERY fast) or just... had more to do, more characters to meet? It's supposed to be a full time job and yet we practically only help with a single case a day. In short, I'll repeat what I've seen a lot of other reviews say; this game had a lot of potential. I almost feel like this could be a demo! I bought it on sale, so it's fine, but for a game that has practically only three hours of gameplay I feel like the price (while probably very justified for the developers), isn't really worth it for people with limited funds, especially since there's no real replayability. If you have the money to spare, sure, it's a fun but short game that isn't too hard, but if you want some challenge or you're trying to figure out what to spend your limited allowance on, this probably isn't it.

name: The Operator

review:
Has promise, but doesn't deliver.

Mechanically there are a handful of things that seem interesting and like you should pay attention to them that just don't go anywhere. There is no real point in taking notes because you are handed solutions to every problem without needing to look around or remember anything.

Cool, I can run programs from my terminal - [spoiler] e.g. I can call certain people if I pay attention to their IP addresses [/spoiler]. But does that come up at all after I'm shown it? No, it's a one-off to get my to type something into the terminal for vibes. Problems are not solveable outside of the linear storyline. Problems and solutions are presented to you side by side. There is no payoff for paying attention to details, because they don't go anywhere, you can't use them to figure anything out. Very much on rails, and a disappointing detective game experience. I almost thought this would go somewhere cool at the end [spoiler] and that you would continue the game as HAL and actually find out who the mysterious baddies are [/spoiler], but this too does not pay off. Just leaves me wanting more, but not in a good way; feels almost like a demo. When it was revealed [spoiler] who the mole was I was like yeah, ok, there are like 6 total people I have met who aren't dead, of course it's my sketchy friend Mike who's been acting weird. [/spoiler]

That being said, individual minigames and puzzles were genuinely fun to solve. I wish the game leaned more into the mechanics and systems they had, I think that is where they were strongest, and made it important and useful to take notes - reward paying attention to the details! review:
This is going to be the oddest negative review I have ever left. This game got me philosophical about reviews: Is a game review to describe whether I think the game is well made? Or is the game review to describe whether I enjoyed it? It's so rare that these two things are out of alignment, I wasn't sure what to write here. I have decided to write a review based on my enjoyment.

So let me just say: This game is well made. It is VERY well made. It's mechanics are a little bit "Papers, Please", a little bit "Clandestine", and a little bit "The Roottrees are Dead" - all meant as a compliment. The production values are top notch. And the story is very well written and very engaging.

And that's where the problem comes in. When a game is this good, my enjoyment hinges on the story being satisfying - and this story is FAR from satisfying. The ending is a cliffhanger that should have been the INTRODUCTION to a game, not a game in itself. And aside from being an incomplete story, the ending is nothing but [spoiler]bad things happening to good people and bad people getting away with it[/spoiler]. And I find that an extremely unsatisfying experience.

So I leave this review to convey an experience for people like me: people who can appreciate a masterfully crafted game that delivers a deeply unsatisfying story. If I'd known how the story ended, I wouldn't have bothered.

review:
My experience with The Operator can be summed up as follows: great presentation, limited investigation.  It's a  game that looks sharp, feels polished, and tells a story that is rather entertaining, yet never quite trusts you enough to truly investigate it on your own. I enjoyed my time with it. I just kept wishing it would let me off the leash.

The production is slick from top to bottom. The performances sell the drama, and the narrative momentum keeps you moving even when a few plot holes start to peek through if you linger too long on the details. It is a fun story. It just is not a particularly demanding one.

Let’s be clear about something. This is not really an investigation game.

You are deliberately guided from one beat to the next with little room to wander or hope oiff the beaten path. That keeps the pacing tight, sure, but it also strips away the thrill of deduction that hallmarks great detective games . No alternate paths, no clever lateral thinking moments, no opportunities to feel like you outsmarted the system. Outside of one genuinely challenging, spoiler free sequence that actually made me pause and think, most of the puzzles feel straightforward and simple to resolve.

And then there is the ending. I assumed I had stumbled into the Bad Ending because of something I had done wrong, only to realize that this was simply... the finish. And I figured it was disappointing.

This game didn't scratch my detective game itch. I love having my detective instincts tested. I enjoy piecing together clues and trusting my logic to guide me. I wanted more depth, more resistance. That said, for someone easing into detective style games for the first time, this is an excellent starting point. As long as you're picking it up on sale.

review:
EDIT: I've been thinking about this a lot, and I just wanted to add one more thing. You can see how I go into quite a bit of initial, just-coming-down-off-finishing-the-game detail down below if you'd like, but I'd like to quickly say here, at the start, that I think a big part of the issue was a fundamental misunderstanding of what this game was. I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game.
I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative.
My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game.
First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once.
The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content.

I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again.

**SPOILERS FOR THE END**

The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. (I saw someone else say that if there HAD been multiple endings, that would also help with the overarching "the game is too short" issue everyone seems to be having, and I agree with that, as well.)
Some people liked the ending, but a lot of people shared the same feelings I have: if I uncover the mystery, am taking notes on the story and correctly piecing together the clues, I want to feel like I 'won' the video game... at least to a degree. But (again, **HUGE SPOILER AHEAD**) it literally doesn't matter at all. Nothing you did, none of the choices you made, mattered. The main character you played dies, every SINGLE one of your contacts/friends dies or goes missing (you cannot save them, it does not matter, and you're informed of their demise in during-credits news clippings, no less), and the only one to escape is HAL, and they're still trying to take down the big bad 30 years later (which is what fans of the ending consider the "silver lining.")
I love when games do some out-of-the-box stuff, but the whole game sets you up like you're uncovering a mystery, exposing a story, and then in the end literally not a lick of it mattered (except that HAL escaped and is still trying, which as far as I can tell, happens no matter what you, as the player, do.) It just felt very forced, and pretty pointless.
Disappointing, because again, some of the mechanics were really neat, and you can tell a lot of love was put into the storytelling aspects.

review:
I would classify this as a short narrative game with very light puzzles.

PUZZLES
A majority of the puzzles are signposted and obvious, and they all give a tutorial vibe. The game will teach you how to solve a particular type of puzzle, but then that type of puzzle is never visited again.

There were two puzzles that weren't, but these felt frustrating as:
- the first one had VERY confusing wording and used terms that were not explained ("tickable" being the word I got stuck on)
- the second one you needed to brute force a solution, which is never fun nor rewarding

NARRATIVE
For a mystery game, the final twist was basically shouted at the beginning of the game and I guessed it within the first 5 minutes. All of the cases pertain to the main mystery (no side missions to divert your attention). When you know the secret right away, it's hard to feel motivated to continue playing.

In the end, I felt it was a shallow, predictable, and simple game. It has good bones, but needed a lot more time in the oven

If a sequel does come along, or this team makes a similar game, I hope they:
- Include more puzzles
- Not make the ending obvious
- Playtest all the puzzles to make sure that things are easily understood and enjoyable (without losing the theme)
- Add in some red herrings/busywork 
- Show off their systems! Similar to a Hypnospace Outlaw or The Roottrees are Dead, have us use the mechanics more than once before moving on to a completely different thing. I would have loved to do more searching, scrubbing, etc in the game but didn't have enough opportunities outside each mechanic's single puzzle.

review:
First of all, let me say that this is a good final product if you see it as a mildly interactive visual novel.

The art direction is great, with the soundscape, voice acting, graphics and beats creating the right atmosphere for a conspiracy thriller.

The problem with it is that it's not a Game. It's a linear railroad that drives you from action to action where you can perform simple, easy puzzles. You don't have any agency, and in most places there is no possibility for branching the story.

Even with a fixed outcome, the developers could have done more with script to give some illusion of agency. The most annoying part is that for every dialog, no matter what is your choice, the outcome of that interaction always the same.

So, play it if you want to watch a conspiracy story with some CSI-type procedural puzzles in the mix.

Avoid if you want to play a game with a minimum of agency.

review:
I really cannot recommend this game. Yes its an Early Access title, still doesn't give it a free pass however.

It runs like hell, performance is maneagable (as much as it is, considering its UE5) and only runs decently if you turn down the settings to anything below Medium. It looks good, yeah but that's the only qualifying factor it has. You can slog through a long tutorial session that's pointlessly 'voice-acted' by a generic Elevenlabs AI script, or you can go on about your way and not do them. Honestly, not doing the tutorial is preferrable. Its got really good grounds for a nice game, but only in the future because right now, it should be avoided.

The game most likely gets way better past the tutorial and the first starting area (which i heavily doubt), but it's not worth the 23€, which even then i felt like i was being robbed considering it was on sale. You can get better games with that pricetag, like; STALKER. Or, The Alters. Hell, go on moddb and get Stalker Anomaly (or GAMMA if you prefer endless torture). Mod either of them, and you have a way better experience than Dreadzone. GOG also offers the service of setting either one up for you for free.

It's saddening to know that for every 1 good game, 20 slop pieces follow like its a cross-country hike. And especially using AI to account for the ''game's general vibes'' is such a lazy excuse.

Need voice actors? Go into a closet or an enclosed space, grab your phone, record some lines; and edit them in FLStudio. It really is not that difficult.

Need art? Plenty of cheap but good artists exist in the world. There are thousands of Telegram channels, Discord servers, & Twitter feeds that have artist hubs where you can hire background artists to make simple but extravagant pieces of work for under 100€. Which shouldn't even be an issue, with the price tag that's been set.

The game needs work, a lot of work before its even acceptable to list it at the current price. I can understand listing it with the price if you are in need of funding, but then state that fact in the main page. Keep the game in the oven for a long time before giving it the full price.

review:
Unfortunately, this game is extremely repetitive. It’s a classic wash, rinse, repeat experience: you keep doing the exact same tasks over and over, with almost no meaningful changes or evolution in gameplay. After just a few hours, you’ve basically seen everything the game has to offer.

The content is very shallow. The real estate mechanics are overly simplistic and lack any real depth or strategic decision-making. Nothing you do feels impactful in the long run — progression is linear, predictable, and boring.

There is also a serious lack of variety:

-> Very limited property types
-> Generic NPCs with no personality
-> Repetitive missions with no surprises or dynamic events
-> A progression system that feels automated and uninspired

NPC AI is weak and often buggy, and the world feels empty and lifeless. There’s no real sense of building or managing a growing real estate empire.

On top of that, the game suffers from:

-> Frequent bugs
-> Clunky or stiff animations
-> Inconsistent performance
-> A very basic, almost mobile-game-like interface

What’s even more disappointing is that all games from this same developer seems exactly the same. They reuse the same graphics, the same environments, and the same overall structure across multiple titles. The only real difference between their games is the set of tasks and the game’s name. It feels like reskinned copies rather than new or improved experiences.

Instead of fixing bugs, adding depth, or meaningfully expanding this game, the developers seem more interested in releasing a Real Estate Simulator 2 and charging players again, leaving this title feeling unfinished and neglected.

In its current state, the game feels more like a prototype than a complete simulator. The idea has potential, but the execution is weak and does not justify the price.

review:
I really wanted to recommend this game because the idea behind it is actually really good. Managing a life-saving serum while exploring a dangerous world was a unique survival mechanic that caught my attention right away. The atmosphere is great, the world looks interesting, and for the first few hours it feels like you're playing something that could become a hidden gem.

Unfortunately, it never became that game.

Like many Early Access titles, it was sold on potential. The game launched as a single-player survival game, but one of the biggest promises was that multiplayer would eventually be added. The developers talked about it, the community was excited for it, and many people bought the game believing it would continue to grow.

Then everything just... stopped.

After months of silence, the developers finally returned in May 2025 with a post called "The Serum Works!" apologizing for the lack of updates. They promised Patch #7 later that year along with the long-awaited multiplayer mode and other improvements.

Patch #7 never released.

Multiplayer never happened.

The communication disappeared again.

I understand indie development is hard. Not every small studio has millions of dollars sitting around waiting to fund years of updates. Games have to sell if developers want to keep working on them. According to estimates, Serum only generated around $120,000 in lifetime revenue, and SteamDB shows the game's all-time peak was just 241 concurrent players. That's an incredibly small player base, and it's easy to imagine the studio running into financial problems. The original developers even sold the IP to Toplitz Productions in 2024.

I don't fault a small studio for struggling financially.

What disappoints me is giving up on the community.

Some of the best indie games today didn't become successful overnight. Project Zomboid, No Man's Sky, Valheim, and even The Planet Crafter all started much smaller than they are today. Their developers kept updating the games, communicating with players, and earning people's trust. As the games improved, more players bought them.

Serum took the opposite path. Communication stopped, promised features never arrived, and the community slowly disappeared. Once players lose confidence that a game is actually being developed, they stop recommending it. Sales slow down even more, the player count drops, and eventually the game fades away.

That's exactly what happened here.

The saddest part is that there really was a good game underneath it all. The survival mechanics were interesting, the atmosphere was enjoyable, and the foundation was there. It simply never got the continued development it needed.

If you're watching YouTube videos from 2024 or reading older reviews, remember those were written when everyone believed this game had a future. Looking at it today in 2026, it feels like an unfinished project that was left behind.

I don't like leaving negative reviews for indie developers because I know how difficult making games can be. But Early Access is built on trust. Players buy into the vision, and in return they expect developers to keep working toward that vision.

Sadly, that trust was broken here.

Great idea. Great atmosphere. Lots of potential.

But potential alone isn't worth buying. Save your money unless development actually resumes.

review:
We took a serious hit. And the first thing I want to say is that many of you were right. Chernobylite 2 entered Early Access too soon. The game needed more time, stronger production stability, and better preparation before being placed in players’ hands. Optimization issues, bugs, temporary voice-overs, unfinished translations, missing polish, and other shortcomings caused some of you to lose trust in us. We understand that. And we are not going to pretend that everything went the way it should have. I am not writing this to look for excuses or to shift blame. I am writing this because rebuilding trust starts with being honest about what happened and then proving, through work, that we know how to fix it.  "I’ve bought a couple of Early Access games over the years. Looking back at them after three years, I have to say it simply wasn't worth it. I have about four games in my library that just didn't make it; the game is completely broken.

My question is: aren't we as players being fooled a bit too much with Early Access nowadays? In my opinion, this concept should honestly be banned. If a developer doesn't have enough money to make a game, they should either wait or they're just out of luck. You shouldn't get rich on the backs of players who work really hard for their money, only to spend it on these kinds of failed projects. This is just my opinion, nothing more, nothing less."

review:
Chernobylite 2: Zone of Exclusion feels like a barely playable demo masquerading as a full game. The world map is vast, but disappointingly hollow. Its emptiness saps any sense of exploration; the experience devolves into mindless fetch quests with little to engage beyond ticking off objectives. Character attributes are mere window dressing - they serve only to unlock dialogue or open locks/containers, offering no meaningful impact on gameplay mechanics.
Combat is unmitigated tedium. Both player and enemy animations are stiff and unresponsive, lacking the fluidity or tactical depth needed for rewarding confrontations. The weaponry arsenal is pitifully limited, with a paltry selection of guns and accessories that feel arbitrary and underdeveloped. The base-building aspect, touted as a highlight, is equally lifeless. Construction feels rote, lacking meaningful progression or creative freedom, resulting in uninspired, sterile settlements.
The game’s core problems stem from a disjointed vision. Systems feel tacked-on rather than cohesive, as if elements from different genres were crudely stitched together. This incoherent Frankenstein’s monster of a game fails to deliver on its survival, exploration, or crafting promises. It’s an underwhelming, unfulfilling experience that squanders its intriguing setting. Avoid unless you enjoy playing extended tech demos riddled with unfinished features and shallow mechanics.
name: Chernobylite 2: Exclusion Zone

review:
The "Identity Crisis" 

I am a massive fan of the first Chernobylite. I considered it a masterpiece because of its haunting atmosphere, tight survival-horror loop, and deep story. However, Chernobylite 2: Exclusion Zone is simply not that experience—not even close.

Where the first game felt grounded and tense, this sequel feels like a generic action-RPG. The move to an open world and the shift to third-person combat has stripped away the claustrophobic dread that made the original so special. Instead of a careful survivalist, you feel like a "superhero" fighting bullet-sponge enemies. It’s heartbreaking to see a series I loved trade its unique identity for a more "mainstream" looter-shooter feel. Truly a massive disappointment for fans of the first game.

The "Mechanical Mismatch" 

I expected a refined version of what made the first game great, but Chernobylite 2 feels like a different franchise entirely. The introduction of classes, "mage-like" radiation abilities, and a heavy focus on loot has turned a gritty survival game into a clunky RPG.

The first game’s companion system and mission structure felt meaningful; here, everything feels diluted by the open-world format. Even the protagonist and the new story direction lack the personal stakes that drove the first journey. If you are looking for the survival-horror magic of the original, you won’t find it here. I hope the developers listen to the community and bring back the grit we actually wanted.

Overall I loved the first Chernobylite, but this is a huge step backward. The game has abandoned the survival-horror and mystery elements that made the original a masterpiece in favor of generic action-RPG mechanics and a bland open world. It feels clunky, the atmosphere is gone, and the new direction is a total miss for me. If you loved the first one for its tension and story, stay away from this one for now.

review:
Bought this game when its name still made sense and the devs were still updating it. We're now well past the 6 month "early access" window, the game can still be beat in about 4 hours once you get past the clunky controls and there's just not a lot to do as the business management sim is fairly mindless with no option to increase difficulty nor any need to buy more than a handful of movies

Maybe I would have recommended it in November but not even a whisper of updates since October and I see HOGO Games has moved onto their next "X Simulator <current year>" game rather than finishing this one

Would love to flip this review around after a future update but currently I'm concerned they're chasing hype trains and hoping to use their studio to pump out AI slop rather than put in the work required to let this game reach its full potential

Edit: True to my word, I played again after the 2026-Aug update. The drive-thru restaurant is a step in the right direction and the pirated movies, while not compelling, at least shows an effort but it's not enough for me to flip my recommendation

Ultimately, I'd like to see the game lean more aggressively into its management sim side rather than just being another clunky physics engine where you stock shelves. This means much better UI on the menus (sorting and filtering options at least), more variable cost expenses and both the ability and a reason to sell/fire unprofitable purchases/employees

Side-note: I'm 95% sure the online ticketing feature doesn't do anything besides take a huge chunk of your capital

review:
I got this game originally and finished it, thought "okay, kinda cozy-slop but a 4/10" But then a lot of the cracks started to show even more when they did the most recent update. This a 2/10 game.
1) A lot of the art assets for paintings are AI, pretty sure some of the splash-screens are too, along with the FMV at the start and the store page image (this was before the disclosures were enforced in Steam).
2) Had a level become almost incompletable because the asset limit on a level was too low or there was a weird memory leak causing it to repeatedly cause a "Fatal error"
3) The contracts system literally STOPS rotating contract types in for you to be able to get some of the achievement contracts like "White Cat" or "In the Family" multiple people have complained and it's VERY obvious this game is nowhere near finished and devs have yet to respond to anyone's concern about these issues.
4) Frequently when in the middle of a job you'll have issues where you're breaking a wall carefully and falling debris will take out a piece of furniture you needed to leave undamaged. 
5) Frequent collision issues out of nowhere and the depth perception when it comes to item placement in your truck is haphazard at best and annoying at worst with weird hitboxes
6) The game would glitch to make all placed interaction hot-spots move down like 20 pixels from their display to some invisible area.
7) The gameplay quickly becomes tedious and finger-numbing with the amount of clicks and need for disassembling an entire house and upgrading your tools BARELY impacts things by more than a 5% margin before capping out at a 25% overall speed improvement
8) The lighting engine sucks eggs making things bounce between the BLINDING reflective light of your flashlight or needing to rely blindly on highlights to disassemble or find things. God forbid you turn a light on in a house or you'd be better off staring at the sun.
9) The time constraints and mechanics around it are also annoying management-wise when it sets an impossible task in front of you like deconstructing a 2 story house in 1 day and the drive time takes half a day?

Overall, save your money. There are better games out there, there is little replay value in this, and it's not fun or even relaxing. It saw the cozy game genre, looked at it, saw how much money it made, stole the formula, but didn't implement it with any thought at all. Guess that's what you get with devs that use AI, lazy, bloated, irritating design that has the charm of sticking your finger in a wall outlet

review:
Quick Note : I really don't like being negative about anything gaming related, but some things have to be said about this Deconstruction Simulator. Sorry if I'm being harsh, I tried my best not to be.


[b]P r o s :[/b]
- Funny concept.
- Watching things blow up is always satisfying.
- Managing the warehouse can be fun... at times.
- Having to deal with garbage can be fun.
- Sending stuff to customers for money is satisfying.


[b]C o n s :[/b]
[b](Gameplay)[/b]
- Get ready to spend 75% of your playtime trying to fit objects inside your vehicle. Being off by a single pixel prevents you from closing the door, which in turn stops you from travelling at all. I would really have enjoyed something more fun (like a loading zone, for exemple, or even something which does not require pixel-precision)

- In the early game, you’ll repeat the exact same two or three missions dozens of times. Some may not mind, but by the third run, the novelty had completely worn off for me (as my interest).

- Time management feels completely arbitrary, mostly due to travel times. If you forget an item - which WILL happen, as you rarely know what you'll need in advance - your entire day will be ruined (on normal mode).

- Game mechanics are sometimes so secret that I had to watch more than 4 hours of youtube videos to discover that there is a button to open the door leading to your factory... and that you have access to it right from the start of the game... I am so glad I dropped my previous save because I only got building contracts, thinking I did not have access to the factory yet ! Same thing with collecting roof tiles from the ground (you can build scaffolding, but you have to buy the right thing for that), or roof plates (which you can almost never get from the ground). Tooltips only appear afterwards, which is not really useful.

- The difference between "Normal" and "Easy" modes boils down to tedious mechanics rather than meaningful gameplay depth: being forced to stop working at precisely 6:00 PM, or pixel-hunting with your cursor to unscrew individual parts. Not particularly engaging design. Not rewarding either.

- Disappearing objects. Invisible walls. Unreachable zones. Basic tools costing three times more than a van. High-pitched sounds made by the most used tools ingame. Customers paying an absurd fraction of an object's cost. Trader on holidays 75% of the time. No way to store items for the factory if not for a contract (no buffer zone). Objects inside customer's vehicule but no accounted for the mission, despite being 100% the correct ones (2 large windows with only one counted, if I remember correctly - although it happened more than once).

- I have seen plenty videos where players seems to have a ton of contracts (10-20) everyday to choose from. I never got more than 4 or 5 daily - and most of the time it's the same ones over and over.

- Persistent bugs (I've yet to experience a single full workday without encountering one). For a paid game officially released nearly a year ago, this is unacceptable. Considering what solo developers achieve nowadays, the state of this product is frankly embarrassing.

- Extremely infuriating moments—for example, picking up roof tiles or roof plates (on a contract's site), only to find the previously full palette almost empty upon return (to homebase). And also, good luck taking on a building contract that requires roof plates when deconstruction contracts with roofs only appear weeks later and you cannot grow stock because of this bug.

- Vehicle management is broken: if you sell a vehicle to buy a larger one, the old one remains in your garage, and you'll still be forced to drive it. If you're lucky, your new (bigger) vehicle won't vanish. Conversely, the starter vehicle disappears as soon as you buy a second one, despite having open garage spots.

- Many contract objectives are poorly explained, and the mission UI is too cramped, making it easy to accidentally destroy items required for completion. Destroy with caution, and carefully don't care.

- House building (Factory) has potential, but being restricted to carrying one item at a time is absurd (especially with unusable trolleys scattered everywhere). The constant back-and-forth travels quickly turns into a chore, which makes the whole factory experience quite boring in the long run. Sad, because it could be so much fun !

[b](Other)[/b]
- I won't even get into the physics engine (half-demolished houses floating mid-air, floating debris you're forced to destroy to complete missions but cannot reach them)... I know, ingame physics depend on the game engine, not your code.

- Having "Unstuck Player" and "Reset Factory" buttons baked directly into the main game menu speaks volumes about the game's stability.

- Graphics won't be judged here, as my GPU is too old to give a fair assessment.

review:
This game can be fun, but the glaring bugs and oversight is a huge eyesore that makes me not want to recommend this game.

Overall the game premise is to deconstruct building, sell of items from deconstruction, and now build buildings (with recent update).

+Positives:
+Destroying buildings are fun and strategic.
+Missions are fun, but flawed (look at negatives)
+Upgrades for tools, warehouse, vehicles, and permits keep players motivated.
+Some of the contract's stories are fun to read.
+Xbox Controller works for the most part involving player movement.
-Negatives:
-Missions will not trigger when completed. (Collecting a certain amount of windows and etc.)
-Items are not labeled correctly, so you will get told your in possession of a stolen item when the mission tells you to take or destroy all items.
-Required Mission item(s) disappear. (Boards, Doors, and Windows), so your reputation will take a hit when you can't complete.
-Missing videos for tutorials!
-Random drops in Frame Rate.
-Bulk Sales are unreliable due to seller ranking system and low cash reward.
-Seller Rank is cutting into profits. Better system would be to set your price and have the customer agree, disagree, or counter.  
-UI is a nightmare for Xbox Controller users (Warehouse, Reading Contracts, and accessing the computer for Contracts and etc.

Overall the game is fun, but the bugs in missions, lacking reward, and terrible UI is why I must not recommend this game at this time. Hopefully, we will receive some updates that will improve the overall quality of the game.

review:
I like the concept and want to like the game. Knowing the dev/publisher (and seeing some early complaints), I waited for 6-7 months to give them sufficient time to iron out major bugs and lack of content due to the game potentially having been rushed. I did not encounter any meaningful bugs, but sadly I still feel let down. The game is not bad: It just isn't fun. For a short 5-10$ game it might have been sufficient, but for 20$ it is not.

The main issue is that the progress does not feel like progress.
- yes, you can buy faster tools
- yes, you can buy more storage-space
- yes, you can get bigger vehicles with more space
- yes, you can unlock permits for bigger contracts 
...but in the end this just affects numbers and not the experience (except for the exoskeleton that is convenient but also not interesting/challenging):
- There are no stories to discover
- There is no concept of location, no areas of operation to unlock or places to revisit
- Selling your goods feels entirely arbitrary so there is no real strategy either
- There is no goal to work towards to

I think the worst part is that houses feel the same. Don't get me wrong, there are different types of houses (small/big, cheap/expensive, damaged...) but they just FEEL the same. The furniture and belongings repeat rather quickly and feel generic. I never felt like walking through a place where people lived / worked - places could look interesting but still feel artificial. Once you have seen a couple houses you have seen them all.

And for the last part, progress is needlessly grindy and slow. And that is me liking grindy games. Taking risks, good thinking and putting in effort/grind should be and feel rewarding. However for a reward to feel rewarding it must serve a purpose and that is missing entirely - you can just do more of the same.

Title: An Analysis of Economic Disconnect in Deconstruction Simulator
Overview
Deconstruction Simulator provides a loop centered on dismantling structures, but it currently faces significant challenges regarding economic balance and progression incentives. While the mechanics are straightforward, the relationship between effort and reward feels disjointed. 
Economic Imbalance
The game features a system for selling salvaged items, yet this process is governed by randomized orders. Because the requirements and payouts are inconsistent, there is no strategic reason to carefully disassemble items. The time investment required for precise deconstruction often does not align with the market value of the resulting materials. 
Gameplay Loop and Tools
The core experience is primarily a "swing a hammer" simulator. Players often find themselves grinding until they can afford the wrecking ball, which renders earlier, more careful methods obsolete. 
Tool Upgrades: By the time upgrades become affordable, the desire to use them for meticulous work has diminished. 
Logistics: There is little incentive to purchase a larger truck; the effort of collecting and transporting larger items is frequently outweighed by the lack of meaningful reward. 
Conclusion
The progression systems in Deconstruction Simulator do not currently offer enough value to justify the more complex mechanics of the game. For players seeking a balanced management experience, the current loop may feel like a repetitive grind without a satisfying payoff.
Rating: Not Recommended

review:
For a game that calls itself Deconstruction Simulator it seems to favor Demolition more (I guess it is a form of deconstruction.) The player's limited warehouse storage coupled with the selling system makes it impossible to store & sell (at least for any kind of a profit) everything you could salvage on a site, spitting on any notion that a player may elect to LARP their company as a eco-friendly company that salvages as much material as possible for re-use.

Storage :
Lets start with the Beam / Plank storage. This shelf could fit like 3 more rows of boards lined up in front of the one row it allows. It also lacks a chain or rope across the front (like halfway up) to prevent the boards from tipping over out of the rack and striking someone seeing as how the safety Inspector is so concerned about your warehouse's safety (more on that next.)

The Safety Inspector. The fact you are inspected after the end of every day and are fined for items not being in a storage slot & these items seized is a complete joke. If I so desired to just pile everything in a pile with no shelves I should be allowed to do so. The real punishment with that would be locating items to sell them with the current sell system. Also a complete joke that this is done when there are several safety issues within the warehouse in the first place with some of the storage.

Sell (Order) System :
This system is absolutely miserable. Pretty much everything you salvage from a contract is going to either A. Not fit in your warehouse or B. Not be requested by the buyers and sit in your warehouse for eternity. The system they added with the trader is a horrible implementation of what the community requested, which was a system to sell off these bulk amounts of extra items, as it penalizes your income the more you try to sell to it.

Additional Notes :
There could also be contracts where instead of having to haul off and resell the materials you salvage it gives you a bonus for the more you successfully salvage for saving them on material costs for the new construction at the site you are working. There could be some pallets set somewhere on the site to deliver the materials to.

Spacebar (Hold) Skip. This should say Continue or Next in basically every instance it is used. Saying Skip implies to me that I will miss something if I elect to do so.

Commercial & Industrial Structures. These would add a nice change of pace from just doing residential structures.

Tile Floors & Walls. We are currently missing the ability to recover these tiles considering we already have the chisel.

Modding Support, A level editor for making contracts to share would be great. Also having a way to add furniture & items to the game so we could further enhance those community made contracts with the proposed editor would be amazing. Vehicles would also be a nice addition but not as big of a deal as the prior items in this comment.

Note: This review is based upon gameplay in Dec, 2025. I do not typically do steam reviews until I have my final impression of a product, and I decided I will not be returning to this title so here are my thoughts.

review:
The game is "ok" through and through.
I never played any simulator stuff on PC and wanted to give it a try. At first, it seemed quite nice: the idea of demolishing houses, move/collect/demolish furniture, manage your own warehouse, sell stuff, upgrade your tools, buy bigger vans, increase your reputation - all nice and dandy. There are four things that absolutely take away from the experience though:

- Cleaning up your mess by collecting all the trash after you "deconstructed" a house. It's super tedious, but a must unfortunately, if you wanna make some cash. 
- Selling stuff from your warehouse. Prices fluctuate a lot and you usually make bad deals.
- You get ridiculous job offers in the "endgame", even if you leveled up everything and have the best reputation. I was expecting lucrative jobs all the time, but vast majority are the lower tier jobs that - guess what!? - require cleaning up the mess afterwards. You know, the tedious stuff.
- The game also seems to be not so well optimized. I have a fairly good pc (NOT the absolute banger, mind you...), but still. GPU usage is almost always maxed out, no matter if I play 1080p or 1440p. This doesn't happen AT ALL in any other game I have. Not even in Cyberpunk 2077 on 1440p and High/Ultra settings... so, yeah.

Nah man, I can't recommend this game. It's ok for what it is - nothing more, nothing less. People who are into simulators might have more fun with this, but if you're like me and never played any simulator before... well, you may be disappointed after 2 hours or so.

Do I regret spending my sweet cash for this game? No.
Why did I spend 20 hours in game? Because I like collecting achievements,

review:
UPDATE:

My original review is below, but I am downgrading this to not recommended. It has a lot of potential, but it is too lazily implemented to get my recommendation. It feels like a game in early, early access and the further you get in to the game, the more unplayable it becomes. 

There are furniture items you can't disassemble, the heavy machinery for deconstruction is completely worthless (because it costs 80% of your contract, and you can just do it for free almost as fast with a hammer). You can't upgrade things like trash collection, so that remains super tedious. And most importantly, the original issue I mention around the salvage/order system being horrible just gets worse and worse and worse. It is SO hard to sell the stuff that you collect to the point where you just give up and smash houses down (with your hammer) to speed run the game so it is over.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

I am giving this a thumbs up, but with a heavy caveat. This game has the potential to be my favourite in the construction/chore simulator genre... except for how aweful the order and salvage system are.

And what is really frustrating is how easy it would be to fix. Allow filtering (or add some clear indicator) for orders where you have sufficient stock. And decrease the penalty for selling to the trader, at least for construction materials, which seem to come up so rarely in comparison to how much you get.

Though those are just quick fixes, realistically the order/salvage system needs to be over hauled (or the cost of advancing vehicles and tools needs to be rethought).

review:
Score: 6.2 / 10

Deconstruction Simulator hits a really satisfying niche: tearing things apart piece by piece while figuring out the smartest way to dismantle each space you’re given. There’s a puzzle-like satisfaction in looking at a house or structure and planning how you’re going to break it down efficiently, and honestly, it’s pretty addicting once you get into the loop.

Controls feel responsive and generally work how you expect them to, and the progression system is fair. Missions eventually become repetitive, but the core gameplay remains enjoyable enough that fans of this type of simulator could easily sink a ton of time into it. For the right audience, this is the kind of game you can keep playing almost endlessly.

The downside is that the cracks start to show over time. The UI is a bit clunky at first, though you eventually learn how to work around it. The visuals and audio are fine but nothing memorable — serviceable, but not something you’ll think about after closing the game.

The real issue, though, is stability.

Bugs are far too common, and worse, some of them are game-breaking. Eventually, my save file ended up bricked with no way to recover it, costing me over a dozen hours of progress. After that, it was hard to justify continuing, no matter how enjoyable the gameplay loop was.

And that’s the frustrating part: there’s a genuinely fun game here, but until the technical problems are addressed, it’s hard to recommend.

Verdict: Not recommended right now. If the developers fix the major bugs, this could easily become a solid pickup, especially on sale.

review:
Unfortunately this game gets boring and easily burnt out VERY quickly.

The start is great, in all fairness: you get to collect high-ticket items, smash things, clean up after the fact, even more smashing, level up your equipment and unlock better houses...

But that's about it for the good. You played a few houses then you've played them all. Why? Let me explain:

- The houses are different in sizes and there are two different types of walls: : wooden walls with plaster, and solid brick wall. Sure, you can knock out the walls and makes the entire house fall (which I admit, sounds soothing and entertaining).But since all houses works the same, it turns "Deconstruction Simulator" into a "Smack this and that wood plank in all walls on all levels" or "smack bottom of all brick walls on all levels" game.

- You're a loot goblin I hear? Good, because you can collect almost every item that's interactable in the game and they are mostly divided into 3 tiers: Common, rare and premium. But oops! You can't really sell them and earn a profit for your efforts because the only thing your customer wants is 25 plaster walls instead of your 4 shelves full of premium furniture and your floor full of premium items like your 4 25-inch TV and your 3 Samsung smart fridges. Saving them until the right order comes through so you can sell them? Sorry, you can't just throw them on the floor of your warehouse, you need to place them in their corresponding facilities, and the warehouse is definitely not big enough to fulfill your loot goblin desires.

(Even if you can sell them to the NPC inside your warehouse, he's so greedy he wants a bigger discount the more items you offer, so all your efforts casually gets a 15% discount instead of the full price it deserves)

- Progression is teeeeeeeediously sloooooooooow. In the game you have to complete x amounts of contracts before you can unlock&purchase the next progression which will unlock more advanced contracts. Sounds fair, SHOULD'VE been fair. Just wait until you have too much money and purchased absolutely every vehicle and tool upgrades in the game, yet your final progression unlock is still 15 contracts away (Mind you, a single house demolition contract usually take around 2 in-game days, which translates to around 1 hour or more of irl time.)

Summary/TLDR: Good at the start, gets really boring and easy to burn out the more you play due to extremely slow progression but too much money, game unable to fulfill your loot goblin desires, and the classic "You played 2 levels, you've played them all".

review:
I can’t recommend Lost Rift at this time. The game has too many issues that directly affect both solo and co‑op play.

Server Problems:  
Multiple times the servers went down, and even in solo I couldn’t start the game at all. That’s not acceptable. When playing with a companion, we also ran into repeated problems trying to join expeditions.

Ammo & Grind Issues:  
The gameplay is fun and challenging, but the ammo situation is awful. The grind to get ammo is insane, and the ammo you spend killing enemies is more than what you can realistically build up. Even on your own island’s danger zone, bow or crossbow only gets you so far. Shotgun guys take multiple headshots, and if you get surrounded — which happens a lot solo or with just one other person — you’re forced to burn ammo. This creates a bad resource loop where you never actually increase your inventory.

Expeditions Punish You Hard:  
You’re basically forced to run expeditions, and if you die, you lose everything. That makes it even harder to recover. You try to build a stack of ammo, but you end up using what little you have just to get it, which puts you right back at square one.

Progression Feels Like Loss Before Gain:  
Story progression might eventually open better options, but the challenge makes it feel like you’re constantly losing ground just to gain a little territory.

Bugs & Building System:  
The game is extremely buggy — major glitches, getting stuck, and the construction system, while likable, is missing a lot of ease‑of‑use features.

Final Verdict:  
Right now, I can’t recommend the game. For a cheap price it might be worth it, but that number needs to be low.

review:
With over 1,000 hours in Rust, mostly on solo/duo servers, I could barely make it through two hours of Lost Rift.

I thought the lack of offline raiding would be something I’d really enjoy. In Rust, losing hours of progress while you’re asleep can be frustrating, so the idea of having a persistent, safe base sounded appealing. Once my base is never under threat, the building system itself needs to be extremely polished, deep, and satisfying.

Lost Rift just isn’t there.

Compared to Rust, the building system feels shallow, the visuals are much simpler, and object placement feels clunky. Because of that, I never developed any attachment to my base. I didn’t care about improving it or keeping it around.

What ultimately killed the game for me, though, was the lack of emergent gameplay during the opening hours. In Rust, even gathering basic resources can turn into an unexpected encounter, fight, chase, alliance, or disaster. Lost Rift’s early game felt far too predictable and uneventful.

And I don’t simply dislike slower games. I have nearly 300 hours in Satisfactory, around 50 in StarRupture, and 80 in Icarus. I’m perfectly happy gathering, crafting, and building when those systems are strong enough to carry the experience.

That’s the fundamental problem here: if you remove the constant threat to the player’s base, the base-building itself has to become one of the game’s major strengths. Right now, Lost Rift removes much of Rust’s tension without replacing it with a building system deep or polished enough to compensate.

review:
I really wanted to like Lost Rift, but after several days of playing with a friend, I'm walking away disappointed.

The biggest issue for me is progression. The food and hunger system feels way too aggressive. You can eat a full meal and feel hungry again just a few minutes later. It becomes a constant struggle to stay fed instead of actually enjoying the game.

Progression also feels heavily tied to PvP islands. To unlock better gear and crafting options, you're basically forced to risk everything you've worked for. If you die, you drop all your gear, including items in your hotbar. On your home island, dying can still cost you everything you're carrying. I don't mind a challenge, but losing absolutely everything over and over again feels more punishing than fun.

The balance between players and enemies also feels off in the early game. Starter-area enemies hit incredibly hard, while basic weapons feel weak and unreliable. The bow doesn't even have a simple aiming dot, and the pistol feels terrible. I've emptied multiple bullets into a single enemy only for it to survive and then kill me in a couple of hits. It's hard to enjoy progression when it feels like you're constantly fighting uphill with weak equipment.
Performance has also been rough. My FPS and latency are often high enough to cause noticeable lag, making combat even more frustrating.
One of the most frustrating moments was spending an entire day gathering coconuts to craft ammunition. Not every tree even drops coconuts, and after all that work I only managed to craft 72 bullets. When I logged in the next day, all of my bullets were gone. Whether it was a bug or something else, it completely killed my motivation to keep playing. My friend and I also need to keep relogging cause  the game glitch out and then u cant chop trees or collect coconuts. I know the game is still new and there will be issues but atm I don't feel too pleased. 
There is also no mini map or an icon on the compass to show where your mates are, plus no fast travel either (but that is something one can still live with)
Even when hosting your own server, the customization options feel limited. Unlike many survival games, you can't rename your server and there are very few settings available to adjust difficulty, progression speed, loot loss, or survival mechanics to match different playstyles.
I understand some players enjoy extremely hardcore survival experiences with full loot loss, harsh penalties, and constant PvP risk. That's perfectly fine. The problem is that Lost Rift doesn't seem to offer much flexibility for players who enjoy survival, base building, exploration, and progression without being punished at every turn.
The game definitely has potential. There are good ideas here, and I can see why some players enjoy it. But between the bugs, performance issues, constant hunger, harsh death penalties, weak starter weapons, and progression being locked behind high-risk PvP content, it simply isn't fun for me.

I'll be stepping away from Lost Rift for now and checking back in the future. Hopefully the developers make some adjustments, because right now the experience feels far more punishing than rewarding.

review:
I bought on sale and I still wouldn't recommend it.

The positives: 
very easy to understand; base building and crafting system are intuitive. 
The combat is fun and good.

The negatives:
Constant crashes in expedition. My PC specs are above recommended, I tried max settings first - crashed. Then tried lowest settings - crashed. No matter what I do it crashes. I get that you can reconnect back to the expedition but crashing mid fight is unmotivating.
Next, on 2 expeditions I heard this annoying helicopter/drilling noise in Western Island. The closer I go towards it the louder it gets. I had to restart my game just to get rid of it.
The overall visuals are great , especially on ultra settings but then I noticed the ground, specifically the sand, it's glitching/showing dark square patches making it unappealing to the eye. Also, the fog is just annoying to play in and  I thought night was bad enough.
Lastly, the game has no player base. I have yet to meet a player in expedition both competitive and cooperative mode.
Personally, it makes no sense to have PvPvE and PvE. I believe that is the reason why no one is playing the game. Why would you separate the player base? To meet expectations to a small demographic? Now, look what it led to; no players. If you are going to be a live service, keep it PvPvE. If you want to cater towards PvE, then don't be a live service, remove PvPvE and just make it offline. You literally alienated a large portion of your targeted audience. I heard this game was only PvPvE when it launched. It could have been great, especially, when extraction shooter games were popping off.
Missed opportunity.

review:
BOY o BOY People Can Fart is back at it again with yet another mixed review live service slop show. I have outriders in my library and had a decent amount of fun with it in a single player capacity, so I figured I'd try this game out for the price of a coffee to see just how buns it was to earn yet another mixed rating on Steam. 

The devs decided to go for the ol chiseled playdough Dishonored/Team Fortress style graphics. It's not bad or anything, just overdone a bit. Ok fine, I can live with it, at least there's ray tracing and ray reconstruction to light that playdough beautifully. 

After spending time in the first island helping this one -legged lesbian named wade and making my generic ugly ass box home with limited build pieces, I begin to realize this game isn't really super focused on base construction and has rather simplistic survival craft elements. "hmmmm w/e maybe it's just early gameplay stuff" I say. Fast forward a bit and i've opened the comm tower and discover some coordinates for a couple more lesbians on the island that can join our butch lady band. Super glad I made a female char at this point cause she's feeling pretty canon, even though I removed her moustache in the char creator that was on by default. 

After Dr Sophia joins our group I couldnt help but feel that we were basically in a lesbian biker gang now and we should call ourselves the dirty dykers, but I couldn't craft a sign to put on my base so the gang died before it formed. Just when I was channeling my inner Sweet Baby Inc. Wade hits me with the news that this game's actually an extraction shooter and not a survival craft game and if I want anything decent to keep crafting more flannel shirts with I better queue up with some other bozos and go loot an island. "oh snap, hold my pride flag, I got this" I said. 

So being as i'mma solo player and don't like online nonsense I choose the solo option to get that proper lone wolf against the elements and the environment experience, right? yeah...wrong! Apparently Solo means you're still forced to play on the island with other solo players even in co-op mode and all of us are competing to loot the same fucking resources and locations? No instanced loot? Several island expeditions in, and my experience is starting to get to me. I'm often joining matches where players have looted the best spots already and i'm having to race against them to check shelves and try to find the same rare crap were all probably after. 

Now i'm understanding where those mixed reviews came from. Mixing Survival Craft ( a genre known for single player, co-op, PVE, Instanced loot, relaxed yet challenging etc.) with an Extraction Shooter (a genre known for multiplayer, PVP, resource scarcity, competition, high stakes, toxicity etc.) is a really bad blend. This game doesn't know who it wants it's target audience to be and thus it gets its divided score. 

For $5 it was a chuckle, and who knows I might put some more time in it for extra laughs, but as it stands right now I think it stinks as a survival craft game and doesn't feel great as an extraction shooter. Give players the option to truly be solo and that would certainly improve the player bases sentiment. There's zero reason for me to be on an island with other solo lesbian cruise ship survivors like myself. There's not enough flannels for all of us to loot. On a positive note, at least wades boat is a Subaru...I think.

03.22.2026:
🌴Lost Rift is a case where trailers and screenshots in the store have nothing to do with reality. The game is in early access, but instead of promising survival and interesting gameplay, it received a dead project with no future. The developers made a huge mistake by betting on online and pvp. In top survival games, the main thing is interaction with the world, cooperative, atmosphere and progress. Lost Rift - has nothing to do with this!

🔸The game world is empty and illogical. These are supposedly islands, but where is the diversity of fauna? Where are the parrots and seagulls, as one bird wants? There is no meditative gameplay, endure the imbalance of damage and armor, as if it were some kind of ARMA 🤮 Hunting and stealth are absent as mechanics. Enemies can see you through walls and dense forests. There is zero logic in their actions, they are just zombies with firearms. Construction is as primitive as possible (floor, wall, ceiling). You can forget about creating beautiful structures. You cannot do basic armor/weapon repairs directly from the inventory, and consumables break very quickly.

🔸You can't customize the open world. The basic settings of all open world survival games are ignored. You can't customize the screen where huge icons turn the screen into a card game. Control settings are not saved, every time I load the game I have to configure everything again. I heard music at the beginning of the game, and then, four hours later, why do I always play in silence, or do I turn on the music? I can't even click on the map to place a marker, the cursor is simply not in this menu! The mini-map on the game screen is completely absent, you just press "M" and look at the png.image.

🔸If you want to get blueprints — go play PVP, and the game says this at the very beginning, as soon as you repair the boat. What PVP? And where are the wonderful islands, adventures and construction that were promised when buying the game? There is no offline mode - you always need to connect to their servers and there is an anti-cheat. But finding live players is a harder task than surviving in an empty game.

🔸 If you're looking for something like Sons of the Forest, Enshrouded, Valheim, with regular enemies and cool building of houses, or the cozy world of Raft - pass by. Lost Rift offers neither. It's a mutant made of poorly working online elements and a completely uninteresting open world. Better buy yourself a coffee with goodies. It will bring you much more pleasure than Lost Rift. A huge discount of 80% is just an attempt to drag at least someone into a project that died before birth.
[hr][/hr]

🔸I will change my attitude towards the game only when someone comes back to reality and starts creating a really interesting game, and makes changes:

⚙️ A beautiful open world. It needs to be worked on.
⚙️ An expanded selection of buildings, for building really great houses.
⚙️ Remove PVP.
⚙️ Optimization is much needed!
⚙️ Reduce the price by half, because the game is not worth what they are asking for it!

⚙️Forget about PVP forever. You started creating Lost Rift, not Hunt Showdown!

🔸The game had a future, and it still has. The game can be great. But I think the time to make the right decisions and changes is running out. Developers, you can be fundamentally stubborn: "we make the game as we see it" Or you can make it for the players, not for yourself.

The visual style is the game's strongest asset. The art direction is genuinely interesting, and the overall presentation creates real atmosphere—even if the underlying graphics feel dated, heavy filters manage to keep things visually coherent.
But the style masks deeper problems. The controls are frustrating and unresponsive, making piloting feel imprecise when precision matters. The gameplay loop relies heavily on grinding and delivery runs, which drains the novelty fast. Worse, the quest design feels genuinely buggy and poorly thought-out—you're not enjoying the game so much as fighting it. It's the kind of friction that makes you feel like you're troubleshooting rather than playing.
An interesting idea and solid aesthetic can only carry so much. The core experience needs tighter controls and better-designed objectives. As it stands, it's a game with potential that gets in its own way.

review:
As much as I loved the game, there are a few sore points about it that prevents me from giving this visually beautiful game a thumbs up.

1. I don't approve of the use of AI to do voice lines for characters. Asides from ethical reason, I think it takes away from the impact characters have on the story. I think if its within the budget the developers should replace it with actual voice actors.

2. Two minigames are kind of annoying. The first one being the taxi boat minigame, its difficult to maneuver in a obnoxious way. I think the difficult controls were partly intentional, but after completing the relevant pilot mission i didn't ever want to replay it with how frustrating it was to just turn, only to go way too far. The second was the deep-sea winch minigame, it was impossible to tell how close or far the sharks and jellyfish were relative to the line, making it really frustrating when i lose the crate because I couldn't judge how close the jellyfish was.

3. Why can't I play the boardgame minigame from my own bar? Why do I have to go to another bar just to play it?

The game is bright and colourful, overall it's a fun experience, perhaps a little repetitive, but I would recommend.
But I can't look past the use of AI. During development using AI is a great way of getting the message across. Placeholder portraits, VA, etc. while building the game and raising funds. However the game has been out long enough now and it's still there. Paying artists for portraits shouldn't be much for just a few busts of characters. If you can't afford VAs then there's nothing wrong with just going back to text.

I'm sorry if it seems pedantic to base my negative review solely on the use of AI, however those are my opinions, and this is the place I choose to voice them.
